text_translated_detailed: From Palembang under date 24th October in the year 1694: experience assists. Always maintain a watchful eye on the activities of Pang Rato, and likewise against any undertaking of Pringabaija, without trusting either of them in the slightest; you are also instructed that upon occurrence of the one or the other to give notice as speedily as shall be possible. with which under the wish of wholesome success I remain with great respect (signed) your service willing friend (was signed) W[illia]m Bolton, on the side In the Dutch Company: Palembang the 4th August in the year 1694. secret. Palembang To the Esteemed: Willem Bolton Merchant, and chief Resident. Earnest, prudent, and very discreet From your esteemed letter under date 4th August last, as well as from the further enclosures, which came secretly into my hands in the Company's common letter, it has become sufficiently clear to me how much trouble their High Worshipful Excellencies at Batavia have taken with the examination of the envoys both from Pringabaija as well as from Pang Rato, in order once to discover the means by which the Jambian [Jambi] miserable condition might be restored or at least its ruin might be prevented and averted: but upon all this nothing being found, except for the last mentioned P[rince] S[outh] Aagje the fortune

Regarding further the conduct and governance of Pangeran Rasoe in Jambi, there has been so much said and spoken back and forth that we know nothing more to answer thereupon than we have done before, it being to be wondered at that the great men of the realm have tolerated this so long, and have not before sought to place his brother Pangeran Pringabaija on the throne or to relieve themselves and their subjects in one way or another from him, the more so as he has made all into enemies, and from each one, if the great men were in earnest about it, would certainly be abandoned. But the complaining and lamenting without wishing to take anything in hand seems to be peculiar to the Jambi people, who apparently would rather see that the Company came to meddle therewith, which we believe was never the intention of your High Excellencies, who solely wish, as we also do from our hearts, that all would go well and the complaining would finally come to an end, to which the prospect still seems wholly uncertain at first, or at least so long as the upland people come to side with Pangeran Pringabaija and remain disobedient. Besides which Yang de Pertuan (his sworn enemy) thereby also gets the opportunity to seek his revenge for the shame he has suffered, and to tie all malcontents to his string, for which loose end Pringabaija will find work enough, meanwhile everything goes to ruin, without anyone thinking about what is best for Jambi and their own welfare. Den 20:e der afgewekene maand gber, en even naar 't afgaan van onsen Jongsten aan VE: p:s vaartuijg van den Costischen Jutie Jong, quam hier boven in desen negorij aan te landen Radin oukir sarij met een gevolg van ses sutx vaartuijgen, en onder die als een expres afgesant met brieven, nevens een mager paart, en een oude gelapte praeuw Jaloor aan Pangeran Ratoe, versoeckende in recompense van dien een Jonge Eliphant, een roer, een dans meijt, een smit, mitsg:s dat Ratomaas Jntan met haar kinderen mogt gelargeert werden een spring soghtje naar Costij te doen, om haar suster Rato maas de pattij te besoecken recommanderende sulthan Dhato ons door een briefje mede 't opsigt l over voorsz: Radin, die maar enelijk herw:ts gekoomen is, om zijn groot vader den ouden Pangeran Drobo, welke verstaan hadde, dat dodel:jk siek was te ontmoeten. Voorsz: gesant op alle de vorenstaande versoecken niets het minste geobtineerd hebbende, is den 3:en Courant weder te rugge gekeert, en op eer gisteren van den radin die naar geen schrijvens van ons wilde waghten gevolgt, en gaat Van Palembang onder dato 20=en februarij A:o 1694. in desselfs geselschap mede over Pangeran dieta ningrat, om mede 't bruijlofs feest van sijn neve kiaijmaes mindelam te helpen bijwoonen: hoe wel kom d'een, en d'ander sulthan Rhato wesen zal, staan VE:s voor ons te ontwaren, en twijffelen niet off haar rapport sal volgens oude gewoonte al wederom met klaghten wegens de sleghte onthalinge, en discoursen van Pangeran Raso vermengt zijn, egter werd de thuijs reijse van gedaghten Radin voor dees keer met wat meerder gerustheijt als op de Jongste voijagie
text_translated_detailed: From Palembang under date of the 20th of February in the year 1694. From Jambi by the under-merchant and Resident Ioannes Reaal, and Council sent to the chief Willem Bolton, and the Council at Palembang. On the 20th of the past month of December, and just after the departure of our youngest to you via the vessel of the Costeese [uncertain: ethnic/regional designation] Jutie Jong, there came to land here in this region Radin Oukir Sarij with a retinue of six vessels, and among those as an express envoy with letters, together with a lean horse and an old patched prau [praeuw: traditional Southeast Asian boat] Jaloor to Pangeran Ratoe, requesting in recompense for that a young elephant, a cannon, a dancing girl, a smith, likewise that Ratomaas Intan with her children might be allowed a short journey to Coste [Costij:] to visit her sister Rato Maas the party, recommending Sultan Dhato to us by a letter also the oversight over aforesaid Radin, who has only recently arrived, to meet his great-grandfather the old Pangeran Drobo, whom he had understood was mortally ill. The aforesaid envoy having obtained nothing whatsoever of all the foregoing requests, on the 3rd of the current month returned again, and yesterday was followed by the Radin who would not wait for any writing from us, and goes from Palembang under date of the 20th of February in the year 1694 in his company likewise over Pangeran Dieta Ningrat, to also help attend the wedding feast of his nephew Kiaijmaes Mindelam: although how the one and the other will be with Sultan Rhato stands for you and us to discern, and we do not doubt that their report will according to old custom again be mixed with complaints regarding the poor reception and discourse of Pangeran Raso, yet the homeward journey of the aforesaid Radin for this time was undertaken and put into effect with somewhat more peace of mind than on the last voyage

Indeed, he had his letter escorted by nearly all the able men of Tobo and a fleet of more than sixty vessels into our sight, where out of respect for the Company, all of them fired their cannon and rowed back upriver. We lived in hope, since they had remained at Pidjoan, which is four miles from here, for more than fourteen days, that upon all our oral and written recommendations made from time to time, something regarding the welfare of Jambi and the reconciliation with his brother Pangeran Ratoe would be negotiated. But after some deliberation, they sent back word orally that Pringabaija had sworn never to reconcile with Pangeran Ratoe, nor to oblige himself to him on account of his father, Sultan Hingalaga. Received on the 23rd of March in the year 1694. From Jambi. On the 10th of March in the year 1694. Batavia. Secret. To the Most Esteemed and Honored Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and Esteemed Lords, Members of the Council of the Dutch Indies. Most Esteemed, Earnest, greatly honored, valiant, wise, prudent, and most generous Lords, your most commanding Lords.

The so frequently rumored envoys in our common affairs to the Palembang residents having finally made an appearance, and at least traveling in the company of an express messenger through Pangeran Ratoe to your most esteemed and honored Excellencies, I have with all possible diligence brought about that for this Commission persons have been appointed on behalf of Pangeran Ratoe, namely Kieij Wadoe Hadje and Sieij Nebbij Wiera Marta, of which the first-mentioned is one of those who also signed the most recent complaint letter through Pangeran Probezz to your most esteemed and honored Excellencies under cover of ours dated the 16th of October of the past year 1693, sent to the Palembang residents. From these persons your most esteemed and honored Excellencies will now be able to learn in secret, as required, the true intentions and dealings of Pangeran Ratoe, as well as how the sentiments of great and small are disposed, and furthermore that without redress from this government of Jambi's municipality, the water which has risen to the lips is standing ready to overflow entirely and to destroy everything. text_translated_detailed: From Jambi under date 10th March Anno 1694. Translation of a Malay letter by Kiai Gede, king of Jambi, to Your High Excellencies, received at Batavia on the 1st of April 1694. This letter is to demonstrate the pure affection, adorned with all honor and respect, coming from Kiai Hede, king of Jambi, to His Excellency the Governor-General and the Esteemed gentlemen councillors of the Dutch Indies at Batavia, et cetera. Furthermore, may Your High Excellencies be informed that now by order of Kiai Gede, the Kiai Wadoudadzij and Angabeij Wiera Marta are being sent to Batavia with this letter, to appear there before Your High Excellencies; and he further makes known to Your Excellency's High Regard how that at the time when Pangerang Area had come to Jambi and had betaken himself with Kiai Gede to the upper lands in order to storm Magonjaja, the Demang Kistjl, as he was then, came to die, and all the peoples of Magonjaja placed themselves under Pangerang Depattij: after which occurrence, this war continued for three more months between the Jambinese and Palembang peoples against those of Magonjaja; but after the passage of that time, envoys from Pangerang Depattij came to Secaij Area and Kiai Gede to request a truce, which they also obtained, and of which a Contract was concluded at Jambi under date 10th March Anno 1694 in the presence of Iang de Pertuan of Pagaroujongh and Iang de Pertuan of Toelanboeang, with Pangerang de Pattij also promising to Kiai Gede with Oaths that as soon as the Palembang peoples had departed, he would then come personally to Tannepillij, recognize Kiai Gede as his legitimate king, and manage the affairs of the realm of Kiai Gede within Jambi; these promises being confirmed with Oaths in the presence of the aforementioned two Iang de Pertuangs.

text_translated_detailed: From Jambi under date 10th March Anno 1694. Translation of a Malay letter by the Pangerangs Porbanagara and Mankopradja, together with the further great men of Jambi to the High Government of India, received at Batavia on the 24th March 1694. This letter is to demonstrate the pure affection, adorned with all honor and respect, coming from the Pangerangs Porbanagara and Mankopradja, together with the further great men of Jambi, to His Excellency the Governor-General and the Esteemed gentlemen councillors of the Dutch Indies residing in the Castle Batavia, et cetera. Furthermore, we make known to the Governor-General and the Esteemed gentlemen councillors of India that Pangerang Depattij, alias Pringabaija, had come with the intention to dispatch his envoys to Batavia to appear before Your Excellency's great regard. Having summoned all the great men of Jambi through his sourowans [uncertain: original term], and proposed to them to summon the Sultan Hingalaga, but they answered him that the summoning of Sultan Hingalaga is not to be despised, when Pangerang Depattij, with Kiai Gede, alias Pangerang Ratoe, would again live in good agreement as before, after that Pangerang de Pattij summoned the Pangerang from Jambi under date 10th March Anno 1694, Katsouma Dijpa to himself, and furthermore had all the Jambinese who had their dwellings above Tannepillij arrested and taken with him, over which conduct the great men of Jambi waited for some time to see what order Kiai Gede would establish or resolve regarding this matter, but nothing good was done in this affair, for Kiai Gede, having only bad companions, believes no one of us all, but follows entirely the counsel of wicked men; therefore Pangerang Porbanagara and all the great men of Jambi make all these aforementioned matters

text_translated_detailed: The letter from the Captain was delivered to Pangerang de Pattij of Jambi on the 10th of March in the year 1694, with proper respect, in which it was stated that the Captain had made known to Pangerang de Pattij that His Honors' Excellencies had requested that he be pleased to come down to Tannepillij, so that together they might resolve matters for the good of Jambi; since all that the Captain said was true, Pangerang de Pattij now also comes down to follow their Excellencies' orders with respect. text_translated_detailed: also held this opinion and wished to do the same, and as proof of this, the Pang Mangongh, together with Keaijdemang Jaja Baija, sent gifts to the Dutch, with a gift of 1000 gantings [a unit of weight] of pepper and two pots of Javanese cloth, which gift was previously mentioned by Pangerang Depatti in that year. Thus that intention was thereby thwarted, and subsequently became the sole and principal cause of the discord that arose between us and Pangerang Depatti. For this reason we are now sending this letter to the captain of Jambi to ask whether he is also inclined to help bring about peace and prosperity in the lands of Jambi. If yes, whatever His Excellency shall resolve regarding this matter for the good, Pangerang Depatti causes us much trouble, and we would not gladly see that we live as friends with the Dutch and Pangerang Ratoe. For this reason we have long been of the intention to ruin the territory of Pangerang Depatti, had we not refrained from doing so out of respect for the Dutch, who have forbidden us to do the same. Now that the Dutch wish to enter into a firm bond of friendship with Jambi under the date of the 10th of March in the year 1694, we shall without doubt come to Jambi. The reason that we do not do so now is because the Jambi district is presently in such a poor condition, whereby trade between us and the Dutch is declining, since we do not have anything to send to the captain as a gift. Thus we shall pray to Almighty God for its prosperity. End. For this reason we are now sending this letter to the captain of Jambi to ask whether he is also inclined to help bring about peace and prosperity in the lands of Jambi. If yes, whatever His Excellency shall resolve regarding this matter for the good, Pangerang Depatti causes us much trouble, and we would not gladly see that we live as friends with the Dutch and Pangerang Ratoe. For this reason we have long been of the intention to ruin the territory of Pangerang Depatti, had we not refrained from doing so out of respect for the Dutch, who have forbidden us to do the same. text_translated_detailed: From Jambi, the 15th of March in the year 1694. To Batavia. To the Most Esteemed and Honored Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords of the Council of the Dutch Indies. Most Esteemed, Earnest, Good-natured, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords, Our Noble and Esteemed Commanding Lords. Dangeran Ratoe's envoy Wadoe Hadji set forth on the 10th of this month with the original, of which the copy is enclosed herewith, and having been escorted by Pangeran Ratoe to the sea harbor, his companion Kieij Nebbij Wiera Marta was seized with burning fever on the way and subsequently became delirious and was brought back. The bearer of this letter, Kieij d'Mang Souranga Marta, letter carrier from Pringabaija, now also undertakes the voyage, his companion Dinang Jaggabaija died of water sickness the day before yesterday and was buried here yesterday. Pangeran of Jambi, the 15th of March in the year 1694. Menduracka, according to the postscript on the original, was wounded with five wounds in his body by one of Pangeran Ratoe's soldiers and can impossibly continue this commission further, complaining most bitterly that Pangeran Ratoe (who gave absolute orders for this work) had so little esteem for him, and that a soldier was granted more privilege to strike a court lady than him, Pangeran Menduracka, who can be reckoned among Pangeran Ratoe's own children in blood. But upon further reflection, and too late, considering that that soldier, and not he Menduracka, has the right of preference for reasons contained in our secret letter, he must console himself with this loss. But how this conduct will encourage the inhabitants of those lands to take refuge there, we leave to the wise judgment of Your Esteemed Excellencies. Yesterday eight fugitives from Tobo arrived, reporting that Pringabaija is sending a considerable number of his people overland toward Iang de Pertuan.

text_translated_detailed: From Jambi dated the 15th of March in the year 1694, concerning Sultan Ingalaga, to which end the Pangerang Pringabaija places his hope and trust entirely next to God upon Your Honour, and upon your good favour, so that Sultan Ingalaga may come again to the fallen city of Jambi, and thereby bring it back to its former prosperity. Yet if it should happen that Sultan Ingalaga does not come to appear in Jambi, then certainly the considerable power of the Company, and also of Your Honour's high regard, will thereby be noticeably diminished, inasmuch as my person has entirely gone astray. Finally, the Pangerang Pringabaija has sent nothing else to the noble lord Director General Joan van Hoorn than merely a hand-ring with gold mounting, with respectful request that this trifle, as a common flower sprig, may be pleased to accept with favour. — Translation of a Malay letter sent by Pangerang Pringabaija from Jambi to the former king of Jambi, Sultan Ingalaga, received in Batavia in April in the year 1694. text_translated_detailed: and Singa Mangala, to appear before Your Majesty and before His Honour the lord Governor General Willem van Outhoorn, with a gift of some pepper to Your Majesty and to His Honour, and also to request of His Honour that Your Majesty might be restored and sent back again to Jambi, for if their high Honours do not deign to restore the person of Your Majesty, then we shall certainly all be lost, and we, Your Majesty's servants, shall have to wander about here and there like scattered sheep, but we hope and pray nothing else from the Almighty God than that we may yet have the fortune to see Your Majesty, whether here or hereafter, for Your Majesty is my lord. Furthermore, I have received with respectfulness Your Majesty's order, stating that I should take Your Majesty's place, but according to my judgment, such a thing cannot happen at this time, even though I had the power of the great Alexander, unless I must first meet Your Majesty, and when there is no occasion for this, then I shall from Jambi dated the 15th of March in the year 1694 — without doubt lose and ruin everything, but I wish to hope for the best; may Your Majesty deign to interpret this saying in the best light, and pardon me along with all Your Majesty's subjects. And may Your Majesty meanwhile work towards what is best, useful and serviceable to us, so that the Company's powerful state in Jambi may remain standing, for which no one else is better suited than the person of Your Majesty and the Governor General, who can restore everything again to a peaceful condition: I beg and request that Your Majesty will excuse me, lowly as I am, inasmuch as I hereby offer to Your Majesty a coyang [measure] of pepper and a gold box, to Ratoe Thirteen pieces of hand-rings,

Furthermore, on the 11th of this month, he appeared before the lodge here; however, your Honored Excellencies' letters were already brought to us on the 1st of this month, in accordance with whose contents we went to audience with Sultan Ratoe within a few days, and spoke with him regarding the increased price of cloth, the winnowing of pepper, the murder of the Company's servant on the Chialoup [small boat] Middelburgh, and the Chinese Iang Zaij that was committed, with such circumspection as your Honored Excellencies' order brings with it, and as the circumstances of the matter on both sides required. However, he has given no final answer to either one or the other, much less has anything been firmly established, contenting himself with many evasions and roundabout ways entirely inapplicable to the matter, and finally referring us with the aforementioned subjects and proposals to Pangeran Arla, who became indisposed that very day. Thus the King has constituted Pangeran Diepa to negotiate with us over these points. However, notwithstanding that we have been in conference with this Pangeran at his house on two distinct occasions regarding this matter, we have (just as before) fished behind the net, and have not made any progress at all, for he differed little from his master's answer, and also did not seem to be authorized in principle to take everything finally upon himself.

Thus, when he happened to be with Pangeran Diepa at the time when we were with him for the last time, we first drew this matter up somewhat from a distance, and regulating ourselves according to the manner of Pangeran Arla, but given the variable hope of the discourses of the present Palembangers, finally the aforementioned Pangeran Diepa made the action of this Radin known in his presence, with such circumstances that both the one and the other had to be convinced, whereupon the aforementioned envoy, wishing to excuse himself, brought nothing forward in his defense except that he had purchased these slaves in Batavia, without being able to indicate from whom, and also without having written proof thereof. From Palembang, the 19th of March, Anno 1694.

text_translated_detailed: 16th of April in the year 1694. This letter was written out of a pure inclination, which is unceasing, from Pangeran Area, realm administrator of the Palembang realm, to the permanent Shahbandar at Batavia, who [Honourable]. Furthermore, may it please the Shahbandar to know that Pangeran Area has now dispatched the Jouragan Sourija with this letter of goodwill to Batavia, in order to trade some pepper there, if the said Sourjangh and his accompanying subordinates through their ignorance and stupidity there should happen to commit some fault, so requests the Pangeran that the Shahbandar may be pleased to hold the same in good regard and to instruct them well. Copy thereof by the Honorable Governor and council at Malacca to the chief and council here dated the 23rd of February last. 6. Since the aforementioned 21st of January, the envoys from Pringabaija have come to us, to their High Excellencies at Batavia, of which so many times mention has been made in our letters to you, and from Pringadaijn, which guests were conveyed by Pringabaija, Dieta Mangala, and other state persons more into our sight, and under the firing of many cannon shots there their dispatches were received, we have had much trouble and strife, living constantly in hope that through him Pringabaija would undertake or carry out something for the common good, but far from that did our aim turn out to fall, particularly when it came to our ears that Seleck Uglaga of Pringabaija, with Pang Ratoe, did not wish to be satisfied. Pang Ratoe resolved to change his intention through Wadoe Hadje to Batavia, but in vain the chiallangs were provided, because as in the text Wadoe Hadje had departed beforehand to Batavia, and from the other mentioned, it goes here beside. From Palembang dated the 10th of April, Year 1694, and that his embassies took place in order to request his Father Sultan Hingalaga from their High Excellencies at Batavia, in order to prevent this as much as possible, Pang Ratoe also could not remain still, but resolved to send forth Kieij Wadoehadje likewise.

text_translated_detailed: In vain the chiallangs were provided, because as in the text Wadoe Hadje had departed beforehand to Batavia, and from the other mentioned, it goes here beside. From Palembang dated the 10th of April, Year 1694, and that his embassies took place in order to request his Father Sultan Hingalaga from their High Excellencies at Batavia, in order to prevent this as much as possible, Pang Ratoe also could not remain still, but resolved to send forth Kieij Wadoehadje likewise, by that means to send, without either of the two having wished to resolve to steer toward the Coast. We have with all possible diligence attempted to dissuade him Pringabaija from this his intention and request, attempted Pringadaija in order to depose his father as yet too untimely, but all has been in vain, so that in order to be no hindrance to this sending, since their High Excellencies have deigned to give license to the same, back the envoys to the Company's pantchis, the envoys have been compelled each one of the Company's present being Pantchiallangs to provide, with which then the aforementioned Wadoehadje on the 10th and Pringabaija's envoy on the 15th of this month or yesterday followed yesterday the voyages have continued forth. What the reason is for the last mentioned their gathering, together with what letters we have exchanged with Pringabaija, Item what thus both by us in common as in secret letter to their High Excellencies regarding all this has been advised, please you from the Copies of that all here beside attached, to examine, to which Copies of that which toward that means in order in this to go briefly, and to avoid double account we have conducted ourselves with all due respect, nevertheless under hope and trust that our actions herein shall be received as well done. Also still enclosed herein a list of 7 persons, whereby it is indicated which are still living and which have deceased, the last two being Jan Isaacsz van Haarlem and Hendrick Pietersz van Greuningen, unknown here, so that you cannot be informed whether they are still living, dead, or where the same are located. With our recently received carpenter who comes to us wonderfully well.

Willem Bolton, and the Council per the Yacht De Peperthuijn [The Pepper Yacht] are sent to Batavia, to their Edel: the high government there. As. No. 1. Original letter from said chief and council dated this day. 2. Duplicate original letter dated the 12th of May of this year per Sir Theunis van Cleeff sent for the first time originally as before. 3. Copy letters by the same dated the 2nd and 8th of June last sent to Jambi. 4. Two of the same by aforesaid chief and council to Malacca sent: dated the 19th of May and 4th of June in the year standing. And 5. Four of the same by the Jambi residents to the aforementioned chief and council, sent: dated the 16th and 22nd of April, 7th of May and 22nd of June last. 6. Answered memorial for the Curator adlites. 7. Four such monster-rolls. 8. Five of these salary accounts together with a vendition roll for said Curator adlites. the purse when with letters and pepper sent to Batavia. From Palembang the 28th of July in the year 1694. No. 9. Requisition of settlements on Jambi. 10. Name roll of certain 17 transferring slaves. 11. Invoice regarding the cargo loaded in the aforementioned Yacht the Peperthuijn. 12. Bill of lading. 13. text_translated_detailed: May, Year 1694, as is expressed therein: in order to fulfill this, we have since then concerned ourselves further with that estate and endeavored also to obtain its remaining goods, which the king upon his murder first managed to get into his hands, such as the sloop or the vessel, a parcel of rice, et cetera, in order to sell them by auction or to send them to Costij, having for that purpose requested Sultan Rato through his sabandhars on two distinct occasions, that since this Chinese was properly seated in Batavia and had only come here for business, and consequently had died under the obedience of the Company here, or rather had been killed, with the addition of several other good reasons, he should therefore also be pleased to hand over those goods to us in order to send them to his Heirs and Creditors to Batavia, and that he, Sultan, having some claim upon Iangzaij, could have the same instituted through us or his envoys to Costij. Yet each time we received in answer that he was also a creditor of this Chinese and undoubtedly one of the principal ones, as he claimed much, but having obtained no payment until now, without however clothing the matter with any probabilities or verifying it with proofs; seeing that in this way nothing was to be obtained, we proceeded in person to him, Sultan Rato, and reclaimed those goods anew and afresh in your Honour's Excellency's name. From Palembang, the 12th of May, Year 1694. on such good and courteous foundations as we deem necessary for the advancement of that matter and for the maintenance of the Company's respect and prerogatives, in which place, instead of thereby achieving our objective, he remained equally unwilling, putting forward various disputes between him and his subjects, which all, or entirely no association

From Palembang, the 12th of May, Anno 1694, we have found and asked Pang Arla to be able to know what the truth of it was, yet we have still not obtained the proper account of it, so that your Lordship's Excellency will be able to receive proper information regarding this in the near future. The assistant Petrus van Voorst, having continued here for some time now and being inclined, with the permission of your Lordship's Excellency, to go to Batavia as a gentleman, has earnestly pressed us to be willing to intercede with your Lordship's Excellency on his behalf and to request permission for that purpose. And since we have no reasons to refuse this, we cannot refrain from presenting this to your Lordship's Excellency with all respect, and together with him to request that your Lordship's Excellency be pleased to meet his desire and fulfill it; in which case we would then gladly be served for the time being with another competent and sober clerk in his place, as we have great need of him. In our request in our last letter to be allowed to extend the bridge, we have neglected it, and we must confess that we erroneously forgot to add that also the palisade around the lodge has begun to decay entirely, and through continuous repair cannot be kept standing much longer and necessarily needs to be renewed, and since it becomes more and more defective the longer it stands, the timber of which it is made being generally rotten and decayed, especially below ground, notwithstanding that it has only stood for three years, we therefore request from you by this letter, your Lordship's Excellency's permission to have the other made of nipa trees, which we find in this swampy ground to be much more durable than the aforementioned timber, for it is a necessary and unavoidable matter which the Honorable Company cannot well avoid much longer to prevent inconveniences at night and otherwise. With this, Esteemed, Honored, Great and Respected, Wise, Provident, and most Generous Gentlemen, we respectfully conclude, commending your Lordship's Excellency to the holy and safe keeping of God, and remain with the wish for the Lord's blessing and our most humble greeting (signed) W. Bolton, J. Bottendorp, on behalf of the Company's Palembang, the 12th of May, Anno 1694.

text_translated_detailed: September in the year 1694. From Palembang on the 18th. Batavia. To the Well-Esteemed Lord, Mr. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords, Councillors of Dutch India. Well-Esteemed, stern, Great-Honourable, Mighty, well-wise, far-seeing, and generous Lord. By the occasion that the Yacht the Blue Mountain, through its long journey between this place and Malacca, had become completely deprived of the necessary drinking water and firewood for some days, and the same not having been able to obtain at the Islands Nanka and Lucipara, was compelled to turn before the wind and seek the Palembang river, in order to provision itself anew there, we have felt obliged to send your High Excellency again to Batavia with 2427 picols [modern equivalent: approximately 145,620 kg] by the Yacht the Andromeda, sent to Jambi with the goods it had. On the 2nd of this month it returned with a small letter. text_translated_detailed: We respectfully report that, contrary to all expectations, at the end of the past month, goods have been brought to us by inland vessels, which Your Honour's esteemed letter of the 18th was previously sent to us per the Chialoup Elisabeth, accompanied by 20 loads of rice for this river, which vessel was unloaded here on the 15th of this month in front of the Company's residence, and was subsequently sent on to Malacca the following day. Desen brief komt uijt een suijpere opregtigh:t des gemoeds van Pang: de pattij anum, aan den nederlandsen resident ten Comptoire Jambij, dewelke seer wijs, verrekende, en discreet is, EE. a Voorts zoo geeft Pang: de pattij bij desen aan den resident te kennen, dat hij den demang narambaija, weder heeft doen afkoomen, vermitsradja boediman den voorn:en denang narambaija, aan hem geschonken heeft, en daar nevens gesonden een brief welkers inhoud Pang: de pattijarum zeer vremd voorquam: zijnde verwonderd dat kiaij gede, de boven landen van Jambij met desselvs negen reviren, aan den koning van maning kabo heeft geschonken, daar hij in geenen deele toe gequalificeert is, en ook gen eijgendom aan die landen eft, also het alles onder des E: Comps=s magt behoordt, en den pang: de pattij selver geen magt heeft, om sijn landen aan andere vorsten over te geven, alle welke zaben den resident zeer wel bekent zijn, wil den kijaij gede, zig zelven met ziel en lighaam aan Radja boediman overgeven dat staat in sijn wil, maar het landt van Jambij behoordalken Van Palembang onder dato 24=en October A:o 169. aan Sulthan ingalaga, en den h:e gouvr=r gener: toe, en hoewvel den panger: de pattij anum bij provisie wel ordre heeft verbregen, om die landen te bestieren, zoo staat egter sijn hoop, en vertrouwen bij dag en nagt op den h:r gouvern:r gener=l, van dewelke hij verwagt dat zijn Ed: de goedheijt zal geleven te hebben, om de poetrij off de koningene wederom na Jambij te steeren dewijle het volk van tannepillij anders ten eeuwigen dagen, tot haar vorige welstandt niet sullen
text_translated_detailed: From Palembang under date of the 21st of October in the year 1694. Translation of a Malay Missive by Pangeran de Pattij Anum, alias Pringabaija to Sir Johannes Reaal, Governor to Jambi aforesaid, received at Batavia on the 6th of November in the year 1694. This letter comes from a sincere uprightness of spirit of Pangeran de Pattij Anum, to the Dutch resident at the Comptoir [trading post] Jambi, who is very wise, calculating, and discreet. Furthermore, Pangeran de Pattij hereby makes known to the resident that he has had the Demang Narambaija brought back again, inasmuch as Raja Budiman has given the aforesaid Demang Narambaija to him, and thereupon sent a letter whose contents Pangeran de Pattij found very strange: being astonished that Kiaij Gede, the upper lands of Jambi with its nine rivers, has given to the King of Maning Kabo, whereas he is in no way qualified for this, and also has no ownership of those lands, since all of it belongs under the Company's power, and Pangeran de Pattij himself has no power to give his lands over to other princes, all which matters the resident is very well acquainted with, if Kiaij Gede wishes to give himself with soul and body over to Raja Budiman, that stands in his will, but the land of Jambi belongs according to [a document] from Palembang under date of the 24th of October in the year 1694, to Sultan Ingalaga and to the honored Governor-General, and although Pangeran de Pattij Anum by provisional order has indeed had orders to govern those lands, yet his hope and trust stands day and night upon the honored Governor-General, from whom he expects that His Excellency will have the goodness to deign to steer the Putri [princess] or the Queen back to Jambi, since the people of Tannepillij otherwise for all eternity shall not come to their former prosperity

text_translated_detailed: From Palembang dated the 21st of October in the year 1694.— Translation of a Malay letter from the king of Minangkabau to the Resident Royal at Jambi, received at Batavia on the 6th of November in the year 1694. This letter of goodwill is sent by Sultan Ibnahimed Syiah, king of Minangkabau, to the resident at Jambi, who is endowed with many virtues, et cetera. Furthermore, the captain should know that his letter of particular goodwill, together with the Demang Narambaija and Astra Souda, has been laid before the feet of His Majesty at a very good and opportune time, in which His Majesty has come to understand that the captain has requested that the uplands of Jambi be restored again to peace and their former splendor and commerce. Regarding this matter, His Majesty has already, by God's blessing, given such proofs as accord with the captain's desire, and furthermore Satourab and Astra Jouda have been dispatched to the captain with the request that the captain send some military force upriver as soon as possible, which the captain promised to do in the month of Ramadan. However, after the aforementioned month of Ramadan and the month of Shawwal had passed until the middle of Dhul-Qi'dah, nothing came of it, from which His Majesty can infer nothing other than that the captain from Palembang dated the 21st of October in the year 1694 is not willing to help settle the disturbances between Kiaij Gede and Pang De Pattij and to improve the uplands of Jambi. Therefore His Majesty sends the Demang Narambaija again downriver with the notification that His Majesty has become reconciled with Pang De Pattij, since there were no other means available to him, as he has waited long enough in vain for the promised military force from the Captain. Deesen brief verbed met heijl en zegen wennelinge, komt van maharadja Batodsiouaan palawan alam sjiah, aan zijn broeder pang: mangkoupradja dis h=a Voorts zoo maak ik mijn broeder bekent dat kijaij gede, door zijn quaat gedoente mijn genoegsaam aantoont der oorlogh te willen aan doen, en zoo de ruineren, het welke aan alle mijn broeders mede bekent is, Ik kan na een naauwkeurig recollement mijner gedaghten niet begrijpen den kiaij gede ergens in „beledigt te hebben, goet, en zijn profeet weten het allenigh wie van ons beijden regt, off onreght heeft; d' oorsaak van dese reden, ontrent mijn broeder is om dat wij van over oude tijden al broeders zijn geweest, en k ook niet twijffele, off uE. zal de broederschap onderhouden, het welke dogh in mijn broeders believen staat, zijnde ik aan mijn kant volkomen gereet, om alles aff te wagten wat van mijn broeders intentie mag wesen, met een volkomen betrouwen op godt, en zijn propheet verklarende wijders nergens aan schuldig te zijn, naar de magt die in de handen mijnes broeders, zoo bij dag, als nagt is, daar hebbe genoegsame blijken van gesien konnende iu mijn broeder zigh wijders toerusten en alles doe, wat met sijn ziinelijkheijt veren komt, hoewel ik hoops dat hij alleen, zonder met Van Palembang onder dato 21:en October A=o 1694. ijmand anders geconjunageert te wesen, zal aankomen, zijnde vorderis mijn broeders meijninge aan mij ten vollen bekent, en ben in godt gerust, schoon dat mijn broeder aan alle kanten mij wil benauwen. fins. text_translated_detailed: From Palembang under date 21st October Anno 1694. Translation of a Malay letter by Siri Maharaja Bato Dsiouaan Palawan Alam Sjiah, to Pangerang Mangkou Pradja, received at Batavia on the 6th of November Anno 1694. This letter comes with blessings and good wishes from Maharaja Batodsiouaan Palawan Alam Sjiah to his brother Pang: Mangkoupradja. Furthermore, I make known to my brother that Kiaij Gede, through his wicked conduct, has shown me sufficient reason to wish to wage war, and thus to ruin him, which is also known to all my brothers. I cannot, upon careful reflection of my thoughts, understand that I have offended Kiaij Gede anywhere. God and his prophet alone know which of us two is right or wrong. The reason for this matter concerning my brother is that we have been brothers since ancient times, and I also do not doubt that Your Excellency will maintain this brotherhood, which indeed lies in my brother's discretion, as I am on my part fully prepared to await whatever may be my brother's intention, with complete trust in God and his prophet, declaring furthermore that I am not guilty of anything, according to the power that lies in my brother's hands, both day and night, of which I have seen sufficient evidence. I can assure my brother to prepare himself and do everything that befits his dignity, although I hope that he alone, without being in conjunction with anyone else from Palembang under date 21st October Anno 1694, shall arrive, and furthermore my brother's intention toward me is fully known to me, and I am at peace in God, even though my brother may press me from all sides. End. Letter, written by Pang: de Pattij Anum to his son Pang: Dieta Ningra to Jambi, received at Batavia

Na toewenschinge van alle heijl, en zeegen, soo laat Pang: de pattij aan sijn soon dieta ningrat weten, hoe dat den selven gelieft te denken aan zijn groot vader pang: porba, dewijle hij den oud vorst is, recommanderende, wijders mijn soon zigh zelver ontrent de volkeren van Tannejillij sodanig te dragen, dat zij daar door verpligt worden, om aan uw alle tekenen van liefde en trouwe wederom te thoomen en zigh inmiddens ten hoogsten te wagten, om d' eerste te wesen, van enige steenen desaanstoots te leggen, dewijle het tegenwoordig een boose en opreerige tijt is, waromme mijn soon wel ophoeden moet wesen om d'orsaak van een quaden naam voor te komen, en alles betragten wat tot een goet eijnde, en een loffelijke gedaghtenis kan strecken, alsoo het niet betamelijk is dat wij den luijster onser lofselijke voor ouderen zoude verduijstere, Ik hebbe geen andere tebenen van bewijs dat nogh leves te thoonen, als dat mijn gebeeden nagt en dag tot welstant van mijn zoon, den hemet op offere, finis.

After wishing all blessings and good fortune, Pang: de Pattij makes known to his son Dieta Ningrat how the same is pleased to think of his great grandfather Pang: Porba, since he is the old prince, recommending furthermore that my son conduct himself toward the peoples of Tannejillij in such a manner that they are thereby obliged to show you all signs of love and loyalty in return, and meanwhile take the greatest care to be the first to avoid laying any stones of discord, since the present time is a wicked and turbulent period, for which reason my son must be very careful to avoid the cause of an evil reputation, and strive for everything that can lead to a good end and a praiseworthy memory, since it is not fitting that we should darken the luster of our praiseworthy forefathers. I have no other signs of proof to show that still lives, except that my prayers night and day are offered to heaven for the welfare of my son. End.

text_translated_detailed: From Palembang under date 21st October in the year 1694. Translation of a Palembang missive by Pang: Pringabaija from the Tambi upper lands, addressed to the Resident at Jambi Joannes Reaal, and received in Batavia on [date illegible] November in the year 1694. This missive comes from a sincere affection on my part, Pang: of the party named Calias Pringabaija, to the Resident on behalf of the Honored Company at Jambi, Sir Joannes Reaal, and so forth. Furthermore, I must hereby make known to the Captain, although he well knows it, that the Pangirang Ratoe was the first instigator who took up arms against Pangirang Mandourakka, which is the same as if he had done it against my person, without distinction. Also, the Captain did not wish to involve himself in the doings of Pangirang Ratoe at the time when he sent a Damang Narangbaija and Astra Jouda with their own armed men up the river and further upstream. But God granted his blessing to the righteous, as the Captain well knows. Concerning the order from Her Excellency's esteemed Highness at Batavia, which Zinga Mangala also brought, it contains that those of us both who first took up arms should not only be declared and held as enemies of the Governor-General, but also of the Netherlands Company. From Palembang under date 21st October in the year 1694. The Pangirang Ratoe has now already twice transgressed this command by taking up his arms against me, Pang: Dipattij Annom, of which the Captain also has knowledge. Furthermore, the Pangirang Ratoe has attempted to conspire together with the people of Ampat Souko Mang:onjaja and Toedjoe Kotta Ilir to ruin me, but this people have revealed and made known this design to me, Pangirang Dipattij Annom (by God's grace), and therefore I, Pangirang Dipattij Annom, then

text_translated_detailed: From Siam dated the 20th of December in the year 1693. This letter comes from the Oija Bercquelangh [uncertain: title/name] to His Excellency the Governor-General Willem van Oushooen [Willem van Outhoorn], and the council of the Dutch Indies. Furthermore, that which Your High Excellency with a gracious inclination per the skipper Marlot has sent to His Royal Majesty, with the request that I should offer the same in all humility, together with also a small letter and a gift to me—we have here on the 12th day of the seventh month in the year 2237 according to the Siamese reckoning received it with great honor and respect, and likewise had the contents of the letter translated into the Siamese language with joy, from which it appears, beyond the oral report made by the aforementioned skipper, that Your High Excellencies are ruling the lands of Batavia still in good condition and peace, over which I am also very much delighted and pleased. I have then laid all of this before His considerable Majesty and at the same time also all the points mentioned in the letter, upon which His Majesty has ordered me that I should provide proper satisfaction to all the clauses cited in Your High Excellencies' letters. Furthermore, in the said missive it is also stated that henceforth all the merchandise which is brought here to Siam and purchased here, together with the silver reals [Spanish silver coins] of the Honored Company from Siam dated the 20th of December in the year 1693, shall be traded and exchanged solely with the treasurer, and in no way with foreign merchants. Cattij, het bestaat in ligoorsen thin 26. baar en2 picols,en sa dende aan haar ho: Edel:s db haar ligoorsen hinzijnde 't selve tot een teken van loutere genegenth:d zulx dat alle poincten off saaken, welke tot den wegh van onderlinge genegenth:, en onversrekelijke vereniging strecken, haar ho: Edelh:s ten vollen bekent zijn, waar aan ons refereren, omme deselve wedersijds te verbeteren op dat het tot den laasten dag toe volstandigh magh blijven, gesz: in de 12:e maand op donderdagh in't Jaar 2237. text_translated_detailed: High Honors such red moris that are stitched or worked crosswise and lengthwise, be pleased to send them back here to Siam dated the 20th of December in the year 1693, to be sold, like those that were purchased by the treasurer. These goods were 15 kin long, to be distributed among all the rajas sammi as a gift or honor cloth, being able to cut 2 garments from one piece, each of 16 kin long, but there would still be 3 kin left over as well of such red garments, like those sent before, which were tight and bright in luster, but those which were now sent were too hastily made, and when they were washed they had no red color, like the others had been. So if your High Honors should send them hereafter, please have them made of 18 kin and 1 cobido [modern equivalent: a unit of length] long, also denser and beautifully red dyed, like those sent here before, then three garments could well be cut from them, each of 6 kin long, to be presented to the rajas sammi as gifts. Your High Honors' gift for this time has been valued at 150 attis silver, his serene majesty recompenses it again with 50 attis more, so that the compensation from his majesty amounts to 200 cattis [modern equivalent: a unit of weight], it consists of licorice tin, 26 bars and 2 picols [modern equivalent: a unit of weight], and thus to your High Honors, as your licorice is here, the same as a token of pure goodwill, such that all points or matters which tend toward the path of mutual goodwill and unbreakable union are fully known to your High Honors, to which we refer, in order to improve them mutually on both sides so that it may remain complete until the last day, written in the 12th month on Thursday in the year 2237, according to the Siamese reckoning, being the current year.

text_translated_detailed: Received by the Chaloupe [small boat] of the Portuguese Domingo de Soisa on the 5th of March 1694. From Siam on the 16th of January in the year 1694. Batavia. To the Noble Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, together with the Esteemed, Honored, Most Respected, Powerful, Wise, Prudent, Most Generous Lords, the High Commanding Lords. After the fluytes [merchant ships] Cronenburg and the Civette Cat had departed on the 27th of November and 20th of December last, both loaded with a cargo consisting of tin, sapanwood, honey, and so forth to the amount of ƒ127,035:17:8 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], namely the fluyte Cronenburg ƒ83,317:— and the Civette ƒ43,718:17:8, together ƒ127,035:17:8. With which vessels we have most humbly presented to Your Esteemed Lordship both in original and in copy regarding the condition of this Comptoir [trading post] and also in detail, and various requests from the King, as the copy of our letter with the aforementioned Civette Cat, attached hereto, from Siam on the 16th of January in the year 1694, further indicates. We had thought nothing other than that you would still be able to receive another parcel, given that little sapanwood was cut this year. Your Esteemed Lordship would receive by the bearer of this, the Portuguese Domingo de Soisa, yet another small portion, as we also stated at that time. From Tonkin, the 2nd of January, Year 1694. The highly esteemed letter of Your Excellencies, honored ones, signed the 20th of June last, came to hand with joy, and we have read the contents with pleasure: the safe arrival of the yacht Boswijk at Costi, as well as our humble letters of the 12th of December brought to Your Excellencies by the English ship via Malacca. That which Your Excellencies in the aforementioned letter have deigned to command us regarding the courts, the governor here, and the order of their High Excellencies' trade in this region, we have followed as much as was possible and within our power, as will be clearly and thoroughly evident in the continuation of this letter through the disclosure of our actions. In order then not to step out of order regarding what has most recently transpired, we shall first show to Your Excellencies, and it shall be our duty with humble respect to begin with the following: how it has come to pass at the delivery of the received gifts to this court of Tonkin with all reasonableness, and we must say that the king was disturbed beyond measure and in a manner difficult to overcome against us, without wishing to give any hearing to right reason or fairness, or allowing himself to be moved by any gift, because this year again no amber had been included in the said Majesty's gift, and besides the sent horses were not to his liking either in form or in age, wherefore he sent them back with harsh orders that the desired same should be sent again according to the king's command and further to Batavia, and through two sent Captains he had inquired how it came to pass that again no amber was for the king, and moreover such poor horses, that the Majesty was excessively disturbed regarding the amber as the principal matter, and would likely deal very badly with us; the answer to this message was that the reason for our answer was that the amber that was coming would be delivered. As for what concerns the state of this kingdom, Your Honors, the same is mostly as it was with the state in rest and peace, except that those from the province of Baauw have raised some difficulties over the refusal of taxes, whereby this king has sent a considerable military force to that region to compel the said rebels to obedience, and has therefore forbidden trade to that province, which comes very badly for our commerce, and the roads and other land routes to China are held very unfree by many roving bandits, which is also very harmful to trade. — Also on the 8th of May there arrived at Tonkin [thaijnangh:] 2. large powerful Chinese pirate junks, which upon their arrival there had seized and taken away some merchant vessels belonging to our people here at home, and drove further there at that place great havoc, whereupon the governor of that province requested the king that the government be provided with greater military strength, whereupon the governor of the east province with a great multitude of galleys and foot soldiers was sent by the king's order to that place, but could accomplish nothing because the said junks upon the arrival of the galleys had pushed deeper into the sea, where the galleys could not follow them,

text_translated_detailed: Regarding the intended departure of the fluyt Westbroek, which has remained here, we have for several months before the arrival of this vessel already sold some goods, both on credit and for cash, though the least amount for ready money, the reason being our hope and good expectations of an ambassador coming from the province of Quanchi after his return, who was sent to this king in order to regain trade through Batavia [Jakarta:] afterwards, but had to return to his land without accomplishing his business. Thus, now that this has been thwarted, we find the aforementioned merchants in considerable difficulty, since they must hold almost everything in hand, so that at present we have no more in stock than 2883/8 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 1,300 kg]. Therefore we remain with Your Excellency requesting 2000 pounds for the coming period. Saltpeter or sulfur—their High Excellencies have desired nothing whatsoever of the least amount today; it appears certain that there is little demand for saltpeter, their magazines must still be sufficiently supplied with it, the demand in general minerals has not been very great, the reason being that the English in the past year brought a considerable quantity with their ship the Pearl, which they sell at the price of 6 and 6½ rix-dollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] per pound, and certainly it is not a price to be despised by a merchant, that he goes there for the same goods and pays the least price, or can get the best bargain, so that we have disposed of a quantity of 5000 pounds both on credit and for cash. What quantity in nutmeg has no demand, but finally another quantity was disposed of. From Tonkin [Tonquín:] on the 11th of November in the year 1694, 8 taels per pound of saltpeter and 4 of sulfur were disposed of, and our remainder, together with what our First Merchant and great judge among them have, amounts to 3756¼ pounds, and the true surplus amounts to 2713¼ pounds, so that we with the approval of Your Excellency are requesting 12500 pounds of saltpeter and 30 to 3500 pounds of sulfur.

text_translated_detailed: From Tonkin under date 11th November, Year 1694. Translation of a Letter from Annam Cok Ongh, that is King of Tonkin, addressed to His Excellency the Lord Governor General Willem van Outhoorn, and to the Esteemed Lords Councillors of India at Batavia. In the past season, Annam Cok Ongh has duly received your Excellency's agreeable Letter, and the presents attached thereto, sent by your hand. And from his mouth, as well as from the letter, greater clarity has come to us, and it has appeared to us as well as it came to our understanding from your Excellency's expressions of a steadfast goodwill and inclination to render us and our kingdom pleasing services and friendships. This has restored us again and brought us some satisfaction, the more so because we do not doubt that your Excellency's subjects must have seen our form of government, which we have brought into practice, for no short time here, and have regarded the same as legitimate. That Annam Cok Ongh has never been unfriendly or unwilling to tolerate foreigners in his kingdom, and to love them equally with his own subjects. From this understanding and experience, many from foreign kingdoms far across the sea have been driven to betake themselves here, and thereby to conduct their trade and profit, just as your Excellency's subjects have done for many years past, and have taken and had proof thereof, which cannot be unknown to them, how among us foreigners are regarded not less, but equally as our own subjects. But why should we write much of this? The deeds must testify to it, and experience will reveal what the true consequence of the matter is. The words must accord with our heartfelt sentiments and meanings, when one shall place firm trust in the dealings of men. And when the words do not accord with the meaning of the heart, there is also no From Tonkin under date 11th

It is known that Tonkin lies far from Batavia. Nevertheless, one knows how to find means to exchange friendship through letters and to maintain it yearly. I have received two letters from you, Excellency, from Annam Cok Setse Tsiantsen Hoe. The content of them was very agreeable to us. But in the latest, your Excellency has expressed your inclination toward us more clearly than before, which has moved me to assist your Excellency's servants remaining here in the land, as much as is possible for me, in their affairs. Although this in the matter of trade is somewhat very difficult for me, nevertheless I shall contribute as much as is required for the continuation of their commerce in this kingdom, provided that they remain under our protection, so that they may dwell among us free from all disturbance and at ease. We shall likewise take similar care for your Excellency's ships, which are sent hither for trade, so that they may not be harmed by any enemies, whether from without or within.

text_translated_detailed:
From Tonkin, dated the 11th of November 1694. Report to His High Excellency the Noble Lord P[eter] Willem van Outhoorn [normalized version: Pieter Willem van Outhoorn], Governor-General, and Your Excellency's Lords of the Council of India, written and delivered by Johannes Liebens concerning his voyage with the 8-gun Yacht the Wind [normalized version: de Windt] to Tonkin upon his return from there back to Batavia [normalized version: Jakarta].

Noble, Esteemed, Courageous, Highly Honored, Wise, Provident, and Most Generous Lords and Noble Governing Lords,

After we had obtained our dismissal from Your Excellency's High Authority on the 28th of June last, in order to navigate with a general yacht to Tonkin, we set sail on the 29th of the same month in company with the designated ships Spier Dijk, Langewijk, Dieren bound for Japan, Verschoondijk, Borssenburgh, and the Nierop bound for Bengal, after having completed the muster under sail, to proceed with our undertaken voyage according to the Sailing Orders and instructions in God's name. And since during the voyage we had fair weather and good progress, we came to land before the Tonkin river on the 18th of July, called the d'Arguaron. However, in approaching the aforementioned coast we suffered an accident through the violent pitching of the small ship, whereby the foremast, which had broken under the ton [uncertain: nautical term], came down from above, and immediately the great main topsail followed, but thank God no one was injured. And in the falling [of the mast], from Tonkin, dated the 11th of November 1694, in the evening we came to anchor on 9 fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 16.5 meters] of sandy ground, firing 4 signal shots at various times to summon the pilot or whoever from the Company's behalf might be at the village of Batza with a letter. On the 19th of the same month, perceiving no one, another signal was given, and noting that this was fruitless and also that we could not exchange vessels with the boat, we found it good on the 20th to, since the weather was foul, send the boat to land to inquire what might be in the way, that no one from the Company's side came aboard. Meanwhile we weighed anchor and moved somewhat closer to 6 fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 11 meters] of water. And since with the setting of the sun still no boat or pilot arrived, we fired three more cannon shots and the marks were also plotted. On the 21st of the same month in the morning with daylight we had a very violent sea from the south, and found ourselves at 5 fathoms of water or near the breakers, driven away. We dared not remain lying there any longer, because the weather was also very violent, and since through the rough sea we saw no chance to weigh anchor, and the matter could not suffer the least delay, it was resolved by unanimous vote in the ship's council to cut the rope in order to get away from the shore, which immediately took effect, and we came then to anchor again on 9 fathoms of sandy ground, to the side of Pearl Island, as becomes more apparent from the resolution drawn up thereof. In the afternoon we fired three more shots to summon the pilot or our boat, but no one appearing, I resolved personally to go ashore (noting that the spring tide was at its height) to undertake whether the pilot could not be brought aboard. Therefore, accompanied by the bookkeeper of the small vessel with the boat.

text_translated_detailed: today desired to arrive within and in the falling of the evening still before the village of Dome at the anchorage by the fluyt [type of ship] Westbroek. When on the 23rd of the same month the Dutchman was dispatched with the papers to the city, and the pilot was recommended to rest, our broken anchor was recovered from the fishing grounds, which he undertook to do, and brought it back to us on the 9th of August. On the 26th of the same month in the morning the skipper of Westbroek came aboard us (having come from above out of the city for the first time to Dome that night), and recounted what difficulties he had endured with his small vessel in laying before the dry ground, since he had not obtained his papers to depart for Batavia until the 5th of January of this year, and because he had absolutely no opportunity of wind to be able to run to sea, so it was decided on the 18th of March, by drawing up a resolution, to run back inside again, just as he still lay here with his full cargo, which consisted of 22,000 pieces of soft and blooming polings, 100 catties [modern equivalent: approximately 60 kg] of musk, 861 pieces of schouerongs, 100 catties of mountain China-brin, 300 catties of amnijs, 30 pots of both salted eggs and preserved [goods]. Item, during the lying in the river it had become very leaky, just as could be seen daily enough, and after we had spent the time of 22 days lying before the village of Dome, so on the 13th of August just before midday the head official S. van Zoo came to us, together with Ongia Ttheeg on behalf of the king and Ongsia Swie on behalf of the prince, the same asking the reason why we had come here, to which in answer it was served that nothing other than to bring the affairs of the Company before the court of His Majesty Van Joncquin [Zhangzhou] under date of the 11th of November in the year 1694 were pending.

Cami [title] here to replace the feared governor Cauwagoets Chitsoeno Cami Samma, and having arrived, their Excellencies together with the committed Sammaoka placed at the old former Fussimano Cami Samma at the very first disposed over many offices that were vacant; and among the same also that of the chief interpreter Skiseijmon (now deceased) who excused himself from that service on account of his illness discreetly: and in his place chosen again, the old former interpreter Croseijmon, who in the year 1667 by the governor Gonnemons [title], together with the departed interpreter Tossojemon, alias Brasman, for some time, was banished from this city, and since then through lack of friends remained without employment, the missing of the same on account of his good conduct above the others, the chief officers of that time were greatly mistreated, as appears from our day register of the date 22nd of September per extract, where also his old and good witnesses are mentioned, we have used him as reporter, interpreter,

text_translated_detailed: What we have been able to learn there regarding the price per picol [unit of weight] has been approximately 270 guilders in silver, and which, aside from the greater value of the silver taels, is still just as much as the Honored Company was able to negotiate for in that same or previous year's season; the reason for this, if truth be told—which we have good reason to doubt—we must declare we cannot understand or reconcile, for the Japanese are not unfamiliar with the Honored Company, which must first obtain it from the hands of the Chinese, and consequently, taking it at the lowest, they should at least not negotiate for less than those who, besides being involved here and being neighbors, would do so, unless one were to suppose and consider that at least those quantities do not fall out larger, and the regents of Nagasaki [Nangasackij] know how to arrange it so that they nevertheless enjoy yearly a considerable portion as a gift from the Honored Company, and consequently they also validate it in their quota at such low prices, and therefore they help suppress the same for their private benefit as much as they can with their power, outwardly subsist, and this year can still be measured nightly: and to confirm regarding the enjoyment of their gift-money comes to light: which position seems to be able to be somewhat strengthened by what was reported to us at the same time, and from various kinds of sold goods on the 13th of September, as specified in the day register, and in which the contrary is to be noted, namely that they for various [goods] received no more, but rather considerably less than the Honored Company obtained, their return cargo, under which 14,000 picols, or 1,750 [uncertain: Ø. lb.] staff copper would run, and furthermore wherever they departed with the same, remains to be read specifically in the Junk book. text_translated_detailed: But in all sorts, the schair or Carmoisin red colors for this place must remain principally excused, and even if it were that there were formerly yearly only 6 to 8 pieces schair woolens, and furthermore among the rest not one of that color more sent, because of the slight use and wear that is made in it, so we judge that it shall suffice to please the great ones, who finally use it for the clothing of the sharp points of their pikes and thunderbusses, to be able to serve them. The distinction of this transaction please your High Excellency note, that the Esteemed Company this year has not only profited half less on the schair woolens, but also on the others, but that they have also received nearly for a single heavy woolen ras as much per sale as for a double schair of the same sort. These remarks shall be able to be discerned and found from the old years also of truth, to be for information. The interpreters from the name of the city burgomasters on the 16th of September, according to a broader account under that date mentioned in the day register, came to warn us that the Japanese measure Ikijen was renewed and a little shorter than the old one was. The same showing us, we found it about ½ ell shorter than the old one, and therefore, although a little room, but 2 /8 @ to reach. We have measured the sold woolens and goods there with in the Batavia more careful speculation. From Japan, the 7th of November, Anno 1694, and since it has just come out, in trust that it shall afterwards also be discerned thus, and against 2 3/8 @ each ikije calculated, shall be able to remain in use and custom. The remaining Chinese pansjes, gilims, and damasks, purchased by your High Excellency at Batavia, the returns thereof have rendered excellently, such as the damasks per hundred 108¼.

You [VE] will well have the apparent opportunity to be able to write with the Chinese junks to Batavia and Siam, and which according to custom it pleases you to observe and remember, though to Siam no more circumstances are to be reported than Her Honors have specially instructed us this year and made known, consisting only in the petition of the various works for the coming year, in accordance with the general letter now departing, without more, as will remain to be explained more broadly thereafter. We undersigned, expressly appointed commissioners, declare that we have collated the foregoing letters and other papers against their originals and found them to accord therewith. Batavia in the Castle on the 31st of January 1695. Boigne V JKlempfonteijne Moen

Time being lacking to accord, allowing the present time not to permit us to answer your high Excellency's aforementioned esteemed missive as required, which however shall be done at the first suitable opportunity, we shall therefore now be brief and respond only on some points. The commissioners of the fluyt were to unload the fluyt and make the division, which was done according to the orders of their high Excellencies. text_translated_detailed: China departs on the 1st of October with Paulo de Figueredo, servant of the English merchant Mr. Standie, to Achin [Acheh] with a sloop and 13 men from Johor. He is given 30 bahars [modern equivalent: approximately 3,600 kg] of harpy fish, 10 [units] of long pepper, 30 [units of] cinnamon, sugar. With this cargo, on the 30th of the same month he departs for Achin. Malacca, the 18th of January, Year 1694. From João Carvalho, Portuguese captain on the ship Saint Joseph, of 300 piculs [modern equivalent: approximately 18,000 kg], carrying 18 pieces of artillery and 20 men, coming from the Philippines. He is given 500 piculs of Manila tobacco, 500 of the same of sulfur. With this cargo, on the 16th of the same month he departs for the Coromandel Coast. The 17th of October: George Jeman, English captain on the ship Roepareel [uncertain: ship name], of 150 tons, carrying 8 pieces of artillery and 30 men, coming from China and wishing to go to Surat. He is given 1,000 piculs of powdered sugar, 1,000 of the same of alum, 30 of the same of quicksilver, and 100 chests of bar copper. With this cargo, on the 21st he sets sail for Surat. The 28th of the same: Albahiet, a Moorish nakhoda [captain of a native vessel], on his ship named Hedrie, of 2,500 piculs, carrying 4 pieces of artillery and 60 men from Diu, wishing to go to Surat. He is given 200 chests of alum, 20 of the same of copper, 200 pieces of spelter [zinc], 20 piculs of elephant tusks, and 20 bahars of tin. With this cargo, on the 11th of January 1694, he sets sail for Surat. Continuation from Malacca, the 18th of January, Year 1694. The 28th of October: Richard, English captain on the royal [ship], agent, carrying 12 pieces of artillery and 70 men, coming and wishing to proceed as before. He is given 220 bahars of tin, 120 chests of copper, 1,000 piculs of spelter, 130 of the same of elephant tusks, 100 of the same of lead, and 10 of the same of eaglewood. With this cargo, plus 10 piculs of powdered sugar purchased here, he departs for Surat on the 6th of January 1694. The 30th of the same: Simão Rodrigo da Silva, Portuguese captain on the ship Nossa Senhora [Our Lady], of 72 lasts [modern equivalent: approximately 72,000 kg], carrying 10 pieces of artillery and 88 men, coming from Macao, wishing to go to Goa. He is given 800 piculs

No. 1. Original missive by and to as above, sealed on today's date. 2. Copy thereof to the aforementioned their High Excellencies, sealed the 18th of January 1694. 3. Three copies of declarations of the first mate and skipper of the fluyt [a type of ship] Walenburg, as well as of 4. commissioners regarding the discovery of a package of palempoeks [a type of fabric]. 4. Translation of a missive from the date Bandhara of Johor to the Honorable van der Beke and Sabandar Pedel, sealed. 5. Memorandum of the debt of the former secretary Pas. 6. Same of private creditors charged to the same with the documents belonging thereto. 7. Map of Malacca's fortress and the stone buildings surrounding it, separately named by Mister the Malaccan freedman Anthony Coresmo, received on the 21st of February in the year 1694, when he was sealed. Declaration of two under-mates regarding their attack against a Malay vessel. 11. Copy of a note whereby the creditors of secretary Pas were enjoined to submit their respective claims within a certain prescribed time. 12. Copy of report of the Sabandar Jacobus Pedel. 8. Application of the Honorable governor Vosburgh to a certain answer delivered by the Honorable Dirk Comans to their High Excellencies, together with the documents pertaining thereto. A. in copy lies herewith, which, having been deliberated upon in council, we have found no reasons to charge the aforementioned ship's officers for the reason why they should charge the damage to account, but rather to leave such to Your Honors' esteemed disposition, becoming more detailed in our resolution, the same having been left to [the decision] of the 20th of December past, most recently in copy sent to Your Honors, to which we shall in this matter refer ourselves with service, and in the meantime remain awaiting Your Honors' good pleasure.

The bleached guinea cloth, which we have previously set at 4½ rixdollars per piece or 90 rixdollars per pack, shall now according to Your Honors' most recent order be no less than 5 rixdollars or 100 rixdollars per pack, against which price the same will certainly sell well, likewise the brown blue guinea cloth against 6½ rixdollars per piece or 130 per pack, which we have also previously set, and which also accords with Your Honors' most recent command.

We have deemed it our deep duty in our letter of the 5th of August of the past year to present to Your Honors what the merchants [were willing to do] regarding the price increase in the markets and against what prices they were willing to accept the aforementioned goods, with the addition of the length and breadth of the same; this being done likewise in testimony of our zeal, to increase, if it were possible, the ordinary Malacca sober profits through the sale of Malay goods, nevertheless the sending of such goods has entirely prevented the cloths there and elsewhere from being sold at a higher price, which certainly must have resulted from necessity and difficulty.

text_translated_detailed:
In April of the past year we have sufficiently set forth the reasons that moved us at that time to request permission from Your Honour's Excellency to visit the vessels that come from the Johorean dato bandhara [local ruler/official], and which shall henceforth pass and repass through here, with Your Honour's Excellency's permission. But since Your Honour's Excellency has been pleased to decline this, we shall not fail to follow Your Honour's Excellency's intention and order accordingly. Having in the successive letters read the successive orders from Your Honour's Excellency regarding what has been said about the voyage of the Johorites, we are also not unaware that the Johorite stands on the books as the Company's oldest ally, and that only in Johor do we negotiate, while the English and the Danes trade there to the great prejudice of Malacca, and we cultivate relations with the same. Your Honour's Excellency's wiser judgment cannot be questioned, as this proceeds from a sincere zeal for the Company's service.

From Malacca, the 11th of February, Year 1794 [uncertain: date appears inconsistent with context].

According to the Contract of the 9th of April 1689, no other European nation may negotiate in Johor except only that of the Dutch Company. Yet this is nonetheless being overridden by them, since the English and the Danes in that region yearly undertake great trade to the prejudice of Malacca's advantages, and bring there a large quantity of opium, cloth, and other goods. It happens also frequently in the world that old allies, through the violation or breaking of contracts on one side or the other, fall into enmity, and through further conference become friends again. Our intention is in no way to offend the Johorite in the least, but on the contrary, we shall maintain with the Johorite, without violation of the Company's dearly acquired reputation, to which trade is principally bound, on our side

text_translated_detailed: From Malacca on the 11th of February in the year 1694, 31st of January: Plahemet, Moorish nachoda [captain/master] on the ship Meheddie, of 50 lasts [modern equivalent: approximately 50 tons] capacity, carrying 3 pieces and 80 cups, belonging to Achinoedij Marican, Moorish merchant, to Coedeloer [Cuddalore], also carrying various merchant goods which he is permitted to carry freely, since they amount to less than his discharged cargo. This letter comes from a good inclination and pure state of Tang De Pertuan, king of Andagireij Dara Salan, to the Honored Lord Gelmer Vosburgh, governor and director of the city and fortress of Malacca, who has much understanding and maintains the law to the benefit of the Honored Company, who preserves the made contracts from Malacca dated the 11th of February in the year 1694, between the Honored Company and her allied friends, who are also well treated and provide assistance to all foreigners who come to his land. The same is wished for him by God: peace, health, and long life. I send Inesie Malacca and Indie Akob with this letter to Your Honors, to make known to Your Honors the certain receipt of your letter sent to me with Maradja Rawan, and with this I have understood with particular pleasure that Your Honors have been pleased to release the aforementioned Rawan with all his people and send him back here, which is truly a sign that Your Honors do not wish to go outside the contract. However, in this I wonder somewhat to learn that (as Your Honors write) all the Andagiresen, whenever they wish to go elsewhere with their vessels, must be properly provided with Company passes. This has not been stipulated in any contract.
