text_translated_detailed: From Malacca dated the 11th of February in the year 1694. Noble Lord Governor, In accordance with Your Excellency's order, I have summoned to my residence the undersigned Datou Bandhara of Patapahan, his handsome son Maradja Dienda, and the young Padoeka Maradja Moeda, who appeared and presented themselves before me, and I have questioned them on Your Excellency's behalf regarding what the reasons for their presence here might be, and what other matters they had to communicate, to which they gave me the following in response. First, they stated that they had come here in order to request from the Noble Company the free passage and trade to Bencoolen [Bengkulu], and from there back and forth to Malacca, without the Johoreans or those from Siaca being able to hinder them in any way or show them hostility. Second, that they wished to be permitted to send a vessel laden with gold and tin here annually, in order to trade cloth in exchange for that mineral. And from Malacca dated the 1st of February in the year 1694. Finally, that since those from Binjei have threatened them with war, they wished to request the Noble Company, by virtue of their mutual alliance, to thwart and resist their harmful and wicked designs, and to support them in all respects. Furthermore, they communicated to me that the Johoreans were pressing hard to break and sever the good friendship between the Noble Company and them, and to abandon all trade, to which the aforementioned Johoreans would incline them by offering that the Noble Company's settlement be removed from Siaca in a short time, and if they did not consent to this but came to refuse it, that in that case they would treat them as enemies in all encounters and inflict all molestation and hostility upon them, requesting

Comans, when the requisition of the aforementioned 30 loads of beans and cadjan dated the 18th of March 1690 was made, had already on the 22nd of August 1689 given orders to Perah to break up the settlement there, which was also carried out, as appears more broadly in the extract attached hereto from the letter sent on that date, and in that same year 1690 the residence of Andragiri was also abandoned, yet notwithstanding that all this is so, the aforementioned D. Therefore it is unreasonable that the aforementioned Mr. Comans should try to shift the responsibility for the Van Malacca [Malacca] under date 11th February, Year 1694, many times mentioned spoiled rice, as well as beans and cadjan [palm-leaf matting], onto my shoulders, for which he is nonetheless responsible himself for the reasons previously indicated. I, with all due respect, judge that Mr. Comans should pay for the aforementioned spoiled grain, as he was the cause of it through negligence, and the Company is not obliged to bear any loss or burden on account of this. And with this I hope that Your Honors will be satisfied on my part concerning the aforementioned spoiled cadjan and beans. But it is remarkable that the said Mr. Comans in his written response mixes my introduction as governor of Malacca with beans and cadjan, and further puts forward without foundation that the aforementioned proposal would have been forced through, which is a notorious shameless untruth and vile slander. Just as Your Honors are obliged in what follows to consider yourselves bound to free me from this blame and to mortify the unjust claims of Mr. Comans. It was then, Your Honors, on the 4th of October 1692, when I reached the Malacca roadstead with the yacht De Beurs [The Purse], where shortly thereafter there appeared on board the chief merchant François van der Beke and Captain Abraham Loot, who had been expressly sent by Mr. the previous governor Dirck Comans to congratulate me and to ask when I intended to go ashore. The answer was as follows: From Malacca under date 11th February, Year 1698, the sooner the better. Shortly thereafter the aforementioned Captain Loot returned to land, whom I recommended to convey my return greeting on my behalf to the aforementioned Mr. Comans, and to request of him that His Honor would be pleased to have the people gather together and prepare everything that could serve for the introduction, since upon my appearance ashore I also wished to be installed immediately, as is further confirmed in the declaration attached hereto granted by Mr. the chief merchant François van der Beeke and Captain Abraham Loot. Shortly after midday I went ashore and came to the ordinary governor's residence, with the militia and free burghers arranged before and beside the gate. I requested Mr. Comans to have the members of the political council come together in a separate room and to have my Commission read there, which was also done in such a manner, whereupon the acceptance and congratulations followed, both from Mr. Comans and the other council members present, without the slightest word of debate or objection. I further requested Mr. Comans to proceed with the public introduction before the common people, to which he showed himself willing at first. text_translated_detailed: the public introduction before the common people, to which he showed himself willing at first. Thereupon we went outside with the entire council onto the square, and the aforementioned Commission was handed to the secretary Jan Pas, and with the people having heard it read publicly, there followed from Malacca under date 1st February, Year 179, not only an extraordinary joyful acceptance from the people, but also such acclamation that many, and likewise various officers of the Company's war fleet lying here in the roadstead heard and observed this with wonder. This entirely contradicts the unfounded claim of Mr. Comans that the aforementioned introduction would have been forced through in an illegitimate manner. Besides, it was clear and apparent to him that my aforementioned Commission clearly contained the authority for me to take up the administration of this government upon my first arrival here, which I was obliged to follow and to obey the said Mr. Comans. It is true that I did not have the duplicate letter from Your Honors read for the introduction, not knowing better whether Mr. Commander Simon van den Bergh had already had the first one delivered to Mr. Comans, but what wrong has been done by this, since the aforementioned letter does not contradict that I should not be installed upon my first arrival? Therefore it seems to me that it still troubles Mr. Comans that he had to step down from his previous authority at that time, for thereby he was deprived of the power to wrong many persons and to make his passion toward them seem justified through an excessively imperious domination. Various persons were at that time from Malacca under date 11th February, Year 1694, held as hostages in their houses (indeed even the Independent fiscal Arnoldus Hackius), who had been placed there on the private authority of the said Mr. Comans. Others had been forcibly sent to Siam and onto the cruising vessels like bandits, without the people knowing what they had done wrong or being convinced thereof. In short, Mr. Comans made sufficient use of his will to carry out his boundless passion as his own law, and played, so to speak, either be silent or burn or help yourself out of the way, so that if there had been no change for the better in the chief administration soon thereafter, or if another person of reasonable governance had not come into play, apparently a great discord would have arisen, both among the free burghers residing here and the Company's servants. Besides, the disputes and double-dealing among the principal Company's ministers had risen to the highest pitch. Indeed, shortly after my arrival here I was also reliably informed that the plan between the aforementioned Mr. Comans and his bosom friend, the secretary Jan Passal then residing here, had been to have Mr. the chief merchant van der Beke and Sabandhaar Gedel both, as well as Mr. the fiscal Hackius held as hostages in their dwellings, and which was not executed after a certain interval, there being no doubt that the aforementioned Pas had incited Mr. Comans to such an intention from Malacca under date 17th February, Year

To whom the chief merchant and provisional governor Dirck Comans shall, upon His Honor's arrival, immediately transfer the entire government and everything that depends upon it, and shall thereafter, together with all other high and low officials, show all deference, respect, and obedience in accordance with the open commission which we have also given to His Honor, so that in conformity with the same, he shall also immediately be presented to the people according to customary practice." Comans that he was not ashamed to bring great contempt upon a member of the high Indian government, believing that he was very slow to relinquish his improper desire to rule, as if he found in it a delectable morsel of great taste. text_translated_detailed: wisdom, will well be able to judge that this government is still quite weak and is occupied with a small number of military men. This statement is to be brought to your Honors by the Honorable Adriaan Lucassen, former chief merchant and second of this government, who has resided here for a considerable number of years. The same has, before his departure, paid into the Company's cash here a sum of eight thousand rixdollars at sixty stuivers each, of which an exchange bill has been granted, so that upon presentation of the same to your Honors' pleasure, the aforementioned Honorable Lucassen may be reimbursed there with an equal sum from the Company's cash. The General Accounting Office of India shall be properly credited in our trade books for the amount thereof, amounting to ƒ24,000 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders]. Here beside lies a sealed missive consigned to the Gentlemen Guardians of the Poor at Batavia, and likewise a set of booklets from the Malacca poor relief office closed in December last, as well as some papers concerning the pay, to be handed over to the chief officer of Batavia's pay office. Herewith then concluding, we commend you, Your Honors Excellencies, with respectful greeting into God's safe keeping, with the assurance that we are, and shall always strive to remain (understood) Well-born, stern, and high commanding gentlemen. Your Excellencies' obedient and submissive servants, P. De Vos Dinaaren (was signed) Gelmer Vosburgh, A. Hackius, A. Loot, and Jacobus Dedel, (at the side stood:) Malacca, the 22nd of March, Year 1694. This letter comes from a good disposition and sincere heart of Gelmer Vosburgh, governor and director of the city and fortress of Malacca with the subordinates thereof.

text_translated_detailed: From Malacca, the 15th of July in the year 1694. Vacant positions, by our resolution of the 14th of August of the previous year regarding the election and selection of the chief merchant [opperkoopm:], second, and head administrator François van der Beke, who was then residing here, to the position of warehouse master [pakhuijs meester], which was assigned to him, and since van der Beke moreover promised to handle the accounting for the warehouse business alone, we found no reasons why the aforementioned mas, being an old bookkeeper and the closest person for the aforementioned position, should not be employed for it. But since your Honors' Excellencies have come to disapprove of this, and we are obliged to obey your Honors' Excellencies' orders regarding salary, we have therefore caused the aforementioned mas to step down from the position of warehouse keeper, and upon the election of the chief merchant Pieter de Vos, we have placed in his place the under-merchant Jan Heij, who was holding the position of shop keeper, which office then fell vacant. And when it was taken into consideration who among the merchants arriving here one might employ for this position, and further having noted your Honors' Excellencies' recommendation to use the aforementioned mas in the secretariat or as a clerk, at least for now, until one has somewhat more proof that one can with confidence leave to him the safekeeping and oversight of the Company's effects. So the aforementioned mas, after serious consideration by the assembled council members, with the confirmation of the governor, has been assigned to the position of shop keeper. The mas is to be inspector, summoned to go with the Blue Mountain over his duties from E. Clerq and secretary of the orphan chamber, deferred in council to the assistant Pieter Vosburgh. The arrival and the part of foreign vessels are inserted in the militia. From Malacca.

text_translated_detailed: The governor Vosburgh declares and testifies in truth, as he has also done before, when in the years 1664 and 1665 he held the position of chief of Cannanore [Kannur], that at that time he saw with his own eyes a considerable number of bezoar stones that were offered to him for sale. On the 10th of March Juragan Oenam, Javanese servant of Sultan Soppe of Chirebon, with a lamboe [type of boat] and 12 men, to Batavia, likewise transporting 100 bundles of binding rattan, of which toll has been paid. 2 packages of copper, 3 of cumin, 1 of Chinese tobacco. text_translated_detailed: Moor Nachoda Calliant sent per the ship Bengale, merchant belonging to the Moor merchant at Surat, namely Beram, of 100 lasts [modern equivalent: approximately 160 tons], carrying 12 pieces and 34 baskets, with which he departs for Siam, also taking with him his brought goods. 44 packs of cloth. 2nd July. From Malacca, the 15th, Year 1694. He also [received] 8 sacks of cumin, 8 of them nutmegs, 3 of them indigo. 22nd March. Nachoda Mia Mahometh commanding the Chialoup [small sailing vessel] of the Moor merchant residing here, Ceden Lebe, with which he has departed for Batavia, transporting 1080 2 pieces of dates, and from here he has paid toll on them. 18 of them manillas tobacco. 17th [date]. The Chinese Thoriona from Padang with his Chialoup and 22 baskets, also taking 10 Coijang [unit of measurement] salt. 18 pieces tobacco. 7½ of them Chinese [tobacco]. From which toll has been paid. 1 gereos [uncertain: possibly a type of measure] 6 of them tea. 4 of them radix China. Chetqua Cindes, resident here, with a Chialoup and 12 baskets, departs for Padang, transporting 3 Coijang salt. 2000 sugar. 10 pieces manillas tobacco. 10 of them powder sugar. From which toll [has been paid] 500 large dishes. 500 half of them. 5 pieces Chinese tobacco. Bauke, resident here, with a chialoup and 6 baskets, transports 8 Coijang salt. 20 pieces manillas tobacco. From which toll has been paid 3 of them powder sugar. 2 of them tea. 10,000 grooved cups. 800 whole dishes. 10 pieces staff iron purchased from the Company, toll-free. From Malacca, the 15th July, Year 1694. 2nd July. Tsanko, Chinese resident here, with a Chialoup and 14 baskets, to Delhi transports 5000 pieces black sugar. 1 [piece]. From which toll has been paid 5 pieces powder [sugar]. From there 3 of them tea. 10 manillas tobacco. 10 chests of gold thread. 1000 half dishes.

Tanhocqua, Chinese resident at Batavia, with a Chialoup and 25 baskets belonging to the Chinese estate of Mr. Tansiouqua, gives 17 Coijang rice and 9 3/8 of them salt, with which on the 5th of June to Achin has departed. 2nd June. Khaijko, Chinese resident at Samarang, with a Chialoup and Chiampan [a type of vessel] with 25 baskets, belonging to the Chinese Captain Quekoenqua at Batavia with a pass from their High Excellencies dated the 14th of May, by which he is licensed to sail over Malacca to Achin, gives 20 lasts of rice, 15 of them salt, 1 piece of clove nails, 2 of them nutmeg, with which on the 5th of the same to Achin has sailed. 3rd June. 4th [entry]. From Malacca, the 15th July, Year 1694. Soeta Prana, servant of Pang Ada, Wilaja [a title], second son of the Sultan, 2nd June. and light breeze, set sail, together with the Chialoupens the Leeuw and the Jager, advanced as much as was possible to us, arrived on the 29th at Bancal, entered the Siaca river on the 30th, passed Zambower (where we learned that the Sabandaar, together with the scribe, had departed upriver with about 30 men to obtain Raja Johon and bring him into his power), continued on, and on the 2nd of April in the evening encountered a prau that advised us that the Sabandaar Raja Johon had been driven away and his praus taken from him by the scribe, who dissuaded us from pursuing that scoundrel, Original letter of this date by and to as above, dispatched. 1½. Copy of letter by and to the above, the 29th July as mentioned. 2. Request for needs and necessities for the coming year. 3. text_translated_detailed: Your Honors: In our most recent humble reports, we have already brought to your attention the complete and sober inventory of the Company's fabrics and cloths present here, and that the collection of tin also had not been very successful. Nevertheless, since that time a reasonable quantity of the aforementioned mineral has come in. However, the current quarter here amounts to 313 2/9 pounds of tin or 221 and 259/4 pounds. We hope that between now and the month of December next, a reasonable quantity will still be able to be collected. We regret that the captains of three Johor vessels, which appeared here at the roadstead on the 16th of this month from the north, and brought with them together forty pounds of tin or 15,000 pounds, have not been willing to sell the same to the Company, whether for cash or on credit, as they are quitting all incoming shipments and passing through by what persons and to whom to reimburse. From Malacca, the 25th of September, Anno 1694. They departed two days thereafter, or on the 18th of the same month, toward Johor, and we shall await your Honors' orders as to where the tin already in stock should be sent, and which we still hope to collect against, or with the arrival of the northern traders shall be sent. The ledgers of the sabandhar [chief treasurer], or the collection of incomes and revenues, having been closed on the last of July past, it appears therefrom that the one and the other amounts to a sum of 14,420 1/2 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders] or 43,261:15 guilders—which our treasury and collection officers and judgment still consider to pass quite well. The murder at Teboealang above Aijerhadja was committed by the orang dagans [foreign traders/outsiders], or foreigners. Raja Aijerhadja wanted to punish some of the orang dagans, but they said they were innocent. Nevertheless, he imposed a fine on them because the foreigners had committed the murder, and according to what the Pounglous [local chiefs] said, this would have been committed multiple times by the foreigners living there, and they would do the same more often if they were not restrained by the imposition of fines. Raja Aijerhadja made known to the Resident that if this matter was not attended to, the people who make the pepper gardens would abandon them. The Resident had recommended to him that he should keep good watch and try to get one of these villains into custody. However, without the knowledge of the Resident, he had mentioned the village of the orang dagans lying in the mountains, and the people from that village had come to complain to the Resident, who had brought this matter before Raja Aijerhadja. May it be given, it would have been, to see the Commander whom Radja Dachelas had captured, and Sultan Becopia driven out of his robber's nests, the cowardly and plundering peoples of the Sapulu Boabandhaars humbled, the Niassers [Niassers:] freed from the violence of the Atchinders [Atchinders:], the expelled peoples of the territory of Segontor and Barram Barram Balantij brought back to their land, the Souboe Alangers brought to peace, the Tigablas Cosas, the weapons which they carried against one another, laid down: The English standing under his command had abandoned Indrapoera; therefore Panglima Radja and the further regents of Padang judged that one ought to receive them with respect, although they brought no letter from their father, so upon their appearance within the fortress of the Honourable Company, they were honored with three cannon shots and a gift to the amount of rixdollars [rixdollars: Dutch East India Company currency] 28½ at export price, half for the general rights account and the other half to be borne by the Honourable Company; all the more so because the regents say they have never been so fortunate that sons of their emperor came to the lower lands, requesting therefore that this deed of ours may be received by Your Honour as well done. — Two English free merchant ships, as we are informed by late writings from Sumatra's West Coast, the 25th of January, Year 1694, have arrived here at Your Honour and departed again. text_translated_detailed: Commander and Panglima Raja, if it is truly their intention to bring Majutta into a good state, that they would then be pleased to order the Esteemed Company's subjects to continue the pepper planting and to separate the Sultan from us, then we would be able to follow the Commander's order; otherwise we fear that the village of Majutta shall be destroyed, and we request that our justice revenues, which we still owe to the Esteemed Company, be given to Padoucca Raja and to Raja Seleman. After the customary compliments, I request of the Esteemed Commander that the 50 rixdollars [modern equivalent: a silver coin of the VOC era] which my son Raja Agmatscha has received from the merchant Hofman at Poulo Hinko [Pulo Cingko] may be charged to my justice account, as well as the two thail [uncertain: possibly a local measure or currency], insofar as the same has been provided by the fiscal to the two authorized representatives of Panglima Raja and Panglima Sire Narra, who were in commission with the fiscal, furthermore I request that the karikon [uncertain: possibly a local official or position] may be given 4 rixdollars monthly for maintenance, for which half may be charged to my account and the other half to the account of the Panglima and the Pounglous [uncertain: possibly a local title or official] of Sillida, finally I request that this letter may be shown to the merchant Hofman, for which I also remain most grateful for that which you have been pleased to grant to my son.

text_translated_detailed: Panglima Chiaija Raja and Panglima Raja have come to know, that the villages in the Siga Blas Cottas, namely Kenarij Moaro Pane, Songi Capaijang, Siroe Kami, Tella Sjoeoa, Canton 't Sirij, Salaijo, Cotto Behara, Cotto Lalang, have taken up arms, and the four villages 't Zilankij, Tanjonge Binkoe, Coentejir, and Soengi Dilouir, subordinate to Cotto Anjo Goegoe, have conquered and destroyed Solor; which is a matter that the Commander and Panglima Raja would have preferred to see otherwise, that the brothers had not come so far as to take up arms against one another. And if there were any dispute about which they could not agree with one another from Sumatra's West Coast under date of the 25th of January in the year 1694, you well know that the Company has always been inclined to allow itself to be used as arbitrators for that purpose. Therefore, to remove all discord, the Commander and Panglima Raja send as their representatives Raja Messouwan and Raja Bilang, [who] will reveal to you the differences. You shall, on behalf of the Commander and Panglimas, bring everything that serves toward peace, so that the thirteen villages may again, as one body and brothers dwelling together, live peacefully with one another. This the Commander and Panglima Raja expect from his good friends, the 10 villages. And when he shall have heard that the 13 villages are again united, he shall be pleased and give thanks to God. [Signed] Abraham Bouden. In the margin: Padang, the 30th of October in the year 1693. — Majutta. Following customary courtesies. To Sultan Mamedchia in Malay. It has been pleasing and agreeable to Commander Abraham Bouden, Panglima Chiaija Raja, to have seen from the letter of Sultan from Sumatra's West Coast under date of the 25th of January in the year 1694.

It has been pleasing and agreeable to Commander Abraham Bouden, Panglima Chiaija Radja, to have seen from the letter of Sultan Mamedchia of the West Coast of Sumatra, dated the 25th of January in the year 1694, that all differences and disputes between Sultan Mamedchia and Radja Adil have been settled and reconciled again, and to confirm this they have sworn an oath upon the Quran, may the good God grant that it may endure eternally. Regarding the sending of 6 or 7 soldiers to secure Sultan Mamedchia's person, so that he will not be attacked by Radja Macoutta and the Malays who side with the English: concerning this, there stands with Radja Manuwassa, whom Sultan Mamedchia has sent with the fiscal, and who has arrived here, to speak further about it, as soon as the Commander has his hands somewhat more free, so that as quickly as possible he may bring news of this to Sultan Mamedchia. The letter from Sultan Mamedchia to be sent to the Governor-General in Batavia has been brought here by the fiscal, and shall be sent with the ship that goes to Batavia. The letter that Sultan Mamedchia has sent to Commander Panglima Chiaija Radja, in which he requests that the 50 rixdollars [modern equivalent: a currency unit of the VOC era] which the Sultan's son Radja Agmetscha received from the merchant Hofman on Pulo Chinco [Pulo Chinco: an island], has been shown to Merchant Hofman; he has understood its contents, and for this he thanks the Sultan for his good care. From the West Coast of Sumatra, dated the 25th of January in the year 1694. This ending with all blessing and grace, wishes to Sultan

text_translated_detailed: In the afternoon we encountered the wind from the north. We were forced to come to anchor under the west coast of Sumatra, dated the 25th of January in the year 1694. We tried to come to anchor at Tengaij, but the wind did not permit it. We came to anchor approximately half a mile outside the shore. We had Pulo Tengaij north-northwest at about a mile from us, and Pulo Meuselaar at the south corner, or the southernmost point from us. To determine the depth, I threw the lead anchor into the ground and hauled it out again. I then found the depth to be 6 fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 36 feet]. We remained lying there until midnight. The wind from the north-northeast made us set sail, and we set our course south-southwest to the west. On Friday the 31st, in the morning with the sunrise, we had Pulo Doendon north-northwest to the west approximately half a mile from us. We held our course, and the wind lasted until midday, when we received the wind from the west-southwest to the west. We held toward the south and had the south corner of Pulo Meuselaar, or to the south, and the north corner of Nias west-southwest from us. In the afternoon the wind turned to the southwest with a stiff breeze. We turned toward Doendon. We could not hold any sail. I made, in my judgment, a lying-to position. Toward evening we received calm with overcast sky, and could see no land. We also maintained calm the entire night. Saturday the 1st of November, in the morning with daylight, I got the north corner of Nias on the compass. I had it from us north-northwest at approximately 6 miles distance from us, and could otherwise see no land. We received the wind north-northwest. I set course to the west. In the forenoon the wind ran north-northwest with a stiff breeze. My [vessel] from Sumatra's west coast, dated the 25th of January in the year 1694. Ship's people

Monday the 3rd of the same month, around 9 o'clock, the king came with a retinue of about 40 to 50 men and asked me what my desire was. I answered him that I wished to purchase rice, beans, and kidney beans [or similar legumes]. If he could help me with that, and if not, then tell me so, for I think I shall depart again. Upon this he answered me: I still have rice standing in the field to dry. Come perhaps. Upon this I went with the nakhoda to that place, but before we departed from the shore, we made a purchase, namely two sacks for one Spanish mat [modern equivalent: a unit of trade cloth]. text_translated_detailed: From Sumatra's West Coast under date 25th January in the year 1694. Report made to the Esteemed and Honorable Mister Abraham Bouden, Commander and supreme authority, and the council of this Sumatra's West Coast, by the under-merchant and fiscal Salomon Vermeeren, concerning his proceedings with respect to the Sultan Mametchia, and Raja Adil at Bantal, and Majutta. Esteemed and Honorable Mister, After I had received my dispatch from Your Esteemed Highness on the 23rd of the previous month, I set out with the full powers of Panglima Raja and the Panglima of Sillida, Siri Narra, together with Raja Ametsa, son, and envoy of the Sultan Mahometchia, and Raja Bongsou, brother and envoy of Raja Adil of Troussan, overland to Sillida, in order to undertake the journey to Majutta. However, since the aforementioned envoys still had matters to attend to at Sillida, and other business to conduct, we had to wait until the 25th thereof, when we set out early in the morning, and we arrived at Aijer Sadja, where we conducted the business we had to do, and on the 30th thereof arrived at Majusta, where I was met by the Sultan Mametchia and the Mentris of that region at the mouth of the river, and from Sumatra's West Coast under date 25th January in the year 1694, was welcomed, and subsequently brought upriver in our pagger [fortified compound], where the Esteemed Sergeant of Wardenburg also came to stay. text_translated_detailed: From Sumatra's West Coast under date 25th January in the year 1694. Report delivered by the East India Company's respectable Lord Abraham Bouden, commander of Sumatra's West Coast, together with his council, handed over by the Bookkeeper Joannes Steur concerning his, together with Panglima Radja's performance as commissioned to Priaman. It was on the 16th of this month towards evening when I received Your Excellency's courteous leave-taking, and my commission was handed to me, whereupon I embarked in a native vessel, and the following day in the evening around 11 o'clock I arrived at the Company's fortress at Priaman; where I found it still in a reasonable state, except for 2 or 3 of the garrison who were somewhat sickly, and after I had sat for a while and rested, it was reported to me by the commanding Corporal Jan van der Veer that three days before my arrival the Company's rice and salt warehouses had been burned by the cannon that fired from one of the small cannons at the front point in the welcoming salute for Panglima Radja's arrival, driven upon them by a strong northwest wind, whereby everything in short (without any attempt at extinguishing) was reduced to coals. text_translated_detailed: From Sumatra's West Coast, dated the 4th of March in the year 1694. The great and small Malays are well-disposed toward him. Furthermore, I have nothing to offer to Your Honour, since I have fallen into a sorrowful state through the death of my son, the Raja Kieetsil. Also, the matter of my other son, who has been appointed as head of Tikoe, has not yet been brought to a conclusion, for there are many people who begrudge him that position. To that end, I request that His Honour would not fail to send over a deed, so that I may rest assured in this matter, and I shall be grateful a thousand times. The bearer of this letter is the handsome son of the Captain of the Chinese here, who, upon inquiry, will be able to provide further information regarding the Padang affairs, for they are known to him. Ending. From Fort York, the 22nd of January, 1694. Sir. Than Riouqua. I have received the [letter] from Your Honour well by nakhoda [captain] Peeko. He had some difficulty with The Boeo, only in that he claimed it belonged to Your Honour. I thought it good to let everything pass. I hope that within a month's time the prau [sailing vessel] will be ready outside the fort. I shall assist Your Honour's prau with pepper, and you may be assured that wherever I can be of help to Your Honour, I shall not fail to do so. I have nothing to offer to Your Honour except only 3 pieces of fine hits for Your Honour's wife. Captain Conko. From Sumatra's West Coast. If Your Honour has need of anything that is in this ship, the skipper shall hand it over to you, whether it be for my account or your account, and I beg Your Honour: if it is possible, send me some good arrack [distilled spirit] by your own prau, and you will be able to expect it and also see how our account stands. Meanwhile, Your Honour's Beloved friend

Your Excellency, [the current approach] is not based on good grounds, but rather builds on incorrect foundations, entirely deviating from the true interest and benefit of the Honored Company on Sumatra's west coast, for the Company is not there in order to become greater and more formidable through an expansion of power and authority, and thus to dominate over all, but rather that through the softening of that harsh manner, through the use of more pleasant and friendly means, one must obtain the advantages in trade and the reduction in burdens and taxes. Esteemed and honorable gentlemen, this is a well-known truth, if we were dealing with people where reason had a place: but it is entirely different with these natives, who, with respect to their faith, must promise every day in the mosque or temple (after divine service is performed) to persecute all those outside their faith until death; secondly, it is a people so curious and full of change that whenever opportunity comes their way, they reject their old friend and take on a new one; thirdly, they are so greedy and avaricious that as soon as someone shows them who gives them something, they take him as their friend, and in doing so the last giver has become their friend; fourthly, we must not imagine that they have love for us, for they have no other love than for gain, and if the Honored Company is to keep these people in hand, there must be respect for the Company's name and a friendly manner toward them maintained, then the advantages in trade will be enjoyed by the Honored Company. That the peace and quiet of the lands, the safety of the roads, and the arrival of sufficient willing merchants is the means by which good trade for the Honored Company can be achieved cannot be denied. Therefore, to obtain the peace and quiet of the lands and safety of the roads, the Commander notes that the means to this end was firmly established by resolution in council of the 10th, 16th, and 27th of December in the year 1692, [which stated] that on this coast the only means was to obtain the same, which (God be praised) has indeed followed from it, and this coast, beginning with Sinkel and ending at Indrapura, the Honored Company now possesses in peace and quiet and safety of the roads. From Sumatra's West Coast, the 21st of May, Year 1694.

does his best and reconciles the parties: but to be accepted as arbitrators, that is the greatest work, and that which is very seldom obtained except through the regard of the Honored Company. The example of the three blas Cottas comes and strengthens us in this, for there everything was in complete disorder and there was no means to satisfy those peoples, so Panglima Raja came to us, and having made this known, requested that we write a letter to those of the three blas Cottas and exhort them to peace, which we then did, and upon which a cessation of arms and also peaceful cohabitation followed: the pepper planting, if one must leave it to the willingness of the native, is little to be expected from it, for five years long they must labor with great expense without enjoying any profit, that is what deters them from pepper planting; but we cannot see the claim that they are dealt with poorly at delivery, for that would have come to our attention before, and until now there have been no complaints about it.

text_translated_detailed: The Commander made known to the Company that he wished to send a letter to Raja d'houlou to invite him to come to Baros to meet with the Commander, so that the matters in question could be settled and they might live again in peace and quiet, which they judged to be a good thing. Thus on the 18th, a Company's bougie [uncertain: type of vessel or canoe] with a Corporal was given the letter for the security of the settlement, to be delivered to Raja d'houlou in the village of Djandie Seriboe (where he was staying), which is located in the Danish mountains, approximately 12 miles from Baros inland. Having arrived there, he handed it over to Raja d'houlou himself and returned with a letter from Raja d'houlou on the 21st. text_translated_detailed: Regarding Ticou, we hear nothing other than that they live peacefully and quietly, and occupy themselves with their agriculture. The pounglous and principal families of Pauw have settled the unrest into which they were brought by Raja Indra.

text_translated_detailed: From Sumatra's West Coast, the 24th of May in the year 1694. At the request made by Panglima Radja, a gift was given to her, especially given the appearance of Sultan Mangsorsa, whom she must receive and greet with great ceremony. The council hopes that this will be graciously approved by Your Honors; and from Indrapoura recently there has arrived 20 bahars [modern equivalent: approximately 2,400 kg] of pepper, which has been delivered to the Esteemed Company by Aijerhadje, whose post Your Honors have likewise deigned to order to be lightened. We shall say nothing further about this, since the English are not only masters of the Majutse kingdom but also sufficiently in control of Indrapoura, so that they will not only take the post at Aijerhadje, but also at Batang Capas, whereby the pepper and gold trade of the Esteemed Company will be cut off. Then Poulo Chinco [normalized version: Pulo Cinta] will remain as a dead body for the Esteemed Company, which the Esteemed gentlemen counselors of India, the Lord van Leene and the Lord Couper, who have been stationed at the west coast of Sumatra, are well acquainted with. And thus it will go the same way with Padang, when the English come to take a post at Priaman, which place has been assigned to them for many years and has been prevented from taking possession by our occupation. Then the west coast of Sumatra will be for the Esteemed Company a heavily garrisoned place without trade. text_translated_detailed: From Sumatra's West Coast under date 21st of May 1694. St. Thomas To Raja de Houlou Following the preceding Compliment in his Malay. This letter comes from the Commander Abraham Bouden, Panglima Haija Raja, to Raja d'Houlou, to make known that he has come to Baros and to hear why Raja d'Houlou has abandoned his Camp and has withdrawn to St. Thomas: If there is misunderstanding and foolishness that has occurred between the children of Raja d'Houlou and some of the Company's servants, that may well have happened without the knowledge of Raja d'Houlou, and in order to understand this, Raja d'Houlou is hereby made known, together with all those who have withdrawn, both nobles as well as common people, that they should appear at Baros before the Commander, to make known the reason for their withdrawal, and having understood those reasons, the Commander will be able to know whether they are innocent, and if found innocent, they can possess their goods again as before, and take up residence and dwelling at Baros. Also, the incident that occurred between the children of Raja d'Houlou and the Company's servants, the Commander will then first be able to know rightly how this foolishness came about, so that he may take such a decision about it. From Sumatra's West Coast under date 21st of May in the year 1644. whereby the peace at Baros remains constant (understood), and was signed Abraham Bouden, in the margin: Baros on the 18th of February in the year 1694. Jange Seriboe To Raja d'Houlou Following the preceding Compliment in his Malay. The Commander Abraham Bouden, Panglima Caija Ladja, has received the letter from Raja d'Houlou, and therein seen the reason which Raja d'Houlou used, why he abandoned the settlement of Baros: as well as that the Oath which Raja d'Houlou has sworn to the Honourable Company has not been broken, the proof of which would be that Raja d'Houlou allows the Batassers with their Benzoin to come to Baros as before for trade. Also, the incident that occurred between the children of Raja d'Houlou and the Company's servants, the Commander will then first be able to know rightly how this foolishness came about, so that he may take such a decision about it. From Sumatra's West Coast under date 21st of May in the year 1644. whereby the peace at Baros remains constant (understood), and was signed Abraham Bouden, in the margin: Baros on the 18th of February in the year 1694. Jange Seriboe To Raja d'Houlou Following the preceding Compliment in his Malay. The Commander Abraham Bouden, Panglima Caija Ladja, has received the letter from Raja d'Houlou, and therein seen the reason which Raja d'Houlou used, why he abandoned the settlement of Baros: as well as that the Oath which Raja d'Houlou has sworn to the Honourable Company has not been broken, the proof of which would be that Raja d'Houlou allows the Batassers with their Benzoin to come to Baros as before for trade. text_translated_detailed: Since d'Houlou, on account of his advanced age, was unfit for governance and withdrew from rule, we thereupon convened the land council and resolved that the perpetrators of the killing of the Company's servants shall retire to Sinkil for so long (provided they shall first have obtained pardon from His Excellencies at Batavia) so that they do not fall into our hands, for otherwise the West Coast of Sumatra [Van Sumatras W„t Cust] under date 25th July in the year 1790 would have to impose the highest punishment upon them, namely Magat Soeke, Pagadon, Pasaloon, Rindoe Kaijoe, Radja Indra, Mage Djalil, and Sisorta. And since the deed was perpetrated by Radja Moeda, whom Radja d'Houlou had appointed as his deputy [wackil] in all matters of governance and to whom he had transferred the rule, on this account the injured majesty has been committed, and he has forfeited all dignities and honors, not only according to common law but also by virtue of the Contract of the Year. So in order to find a middle way and not to utterly destroy the lineage of Radja d'Houlou insofar as they are innocent of this deed, it has been decided to annul the dignity of Radja d'Houlou as Radja d'Houlou, and to place the governance in one head, together with four pounglous [pounglou: a regional administrator or chief], under the name of Radja Baros, chief regent, and Orang Kaija Soudagar [merchant chief], First Pounglou; Orang Kaija Baleij, Second Pounglou; Maradja Moeda, Third; and Radja Sittia Moeda, Fourth. All the Battassers and Baroese shall take the oath of loyalty to Radja Baros, both those of Radja d'Houlou and those of Radja d'Hheer, in order thereby to remove the disputes about whether one belongs to Radja d'Houlou's or Radja d'Hheer's people, and likewise in the slaughtering of buffalo, to show honor to none but Radja Baros. Furthermore, such rights as were exercised in particular toward Radja d'Houlou or Radja d'Hheer shall pass to Radja Baros, and in order to make no distinction between persons or villages, the peoples, pounglous, and radjas shall dwell together in one village, and that shall be called by the name of Village Baros. The further contracts are renewed insofar as this does not come to contradict them, and furthermore shall be sworn to, whereupon it shall follow that each one shall be given back what he has lost, insofar as it still exists, and all those who have fled beyond the aforementioned persons shall be permitted to return to their dwellings. Thus the Radjas have deemed it good to recognize Radja d'Hheer as Radja Baros, and Radja Manuwersa as Orang Caija Soudagar, or First Pounglou; Sire Narra, Orang Kaija Baleij, or Second Pounglou; Bacampal, Maradja Moeda, Third Pounglou; and Radja Dekara, Sittia Moeda, Fourth Pounglou. Translation of a letter from Radja d'Houlou from the village Sangi Seriboe, lying in the mountains, to the Esteemed Commander Abraham Bouden, Commander of this West Coast of Sumatra, sent to Baros on the 2nd of February 1694.

After the customary Malay preceding compliments. The letter from the Esteemed Commander Panglima Crataija Radja, sent under date 21st May 1694, has been received by me. Its contents being directed to make me understand the reason for my flight from the village Baros. So it is: six Hollanders, together with Bacampal, came to the house of Radja Moeda, called Radja Moeda, together with his son called Maraoetang, and his brother-in-law Maget Dadang, and moreover another woman was shot dead. Having heard this rumor, I immediately went to the dwelling of Radja Moeda, but on the way over a bridge I fell to the ground. Having seen this, they picked me up and brought me to Aijer Mamoesar. Having arrived there, I was subsequently brought by the Battassers to Saint Thomas. This then is the reason why I fled from the Village Baros, all of which and more

This then is the reason why I fled from the Village Baros, all of which and more is also known to Radja Lele Sittia, Radja Bandhara, and Bhandara Radja. It has now been three years, during which time I have always been sickly, for which reason I have not been able to come within the Company's fortress, and therefore it was approved by the resident Mortier that I place my son Radja Moeda as my deputy in my place. Yet if any serious negotiations should arise, I should then also be given notice of them. Well, the time has passed, and if any injustice has been done by [West Coast of Sumatra [Van Sumatras W=t Cust] under date 24th May in the year 1694] my son Radja Moeda, he has come along, and also has done nothing unjust to my knowledge. And if Radja Moeda had undertaken anything improper toward the resident, it would nonetheless have been proper that I be warned of it beforehand, but regarding this occurrence not the least notice was given to me. I have nothing in the world to serve as a present for the Esteemed Commander Panglima Chahaija Radja. My buffalo, which run along the seashore to Baros, I will gladly have given as provisions for the soldiers, which they may then simply demand. An oath that I owe to the Esteemed Company shall never again be broken by me. Until now I have kept myself in the Village Sangi Seriboe, and I send the Battassers with their benzoin to trade.

text_translated_detailed: Of Sumatra's West Coast under date of the 21st of May in the year 1694. Articles of a further bond concluded and made between the general Dutch chartered East India Company on the one hand, and the government of Baros on the other hand by Abraham Bouden, Commander and supreme officer on and along Sumatra's west coast strand lands, stadtholder both of the Manincabousen king as of the Honored Company in the name of the Noble Lord Willem Van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Noble Lords Councillors of India, representing the high government and supreme authority on behalf of the aforementioned Company, with Raja the Lord as Raja Baros, Raja Miniassa, grandson of Raja d'Houlou, and commissioned by the same as first Poungul or orang kaij soudagare [chief merchant], Sirre Narra as second Poungul or Orangkaij baleij, Bacampal as third Poungul or Maharaja Moeda, Raja de Kara as fourth or last Poungul or Sitia Moeda, reading as follows. First Article That the government of Baros, beginning in the north with Sinkel and ending in the south with Bathan, shall henceforth consist of one king and four Pounglous [Pungulus: local chiefs] for the removal of disputes, riots, conspiracies, evil crimes, famines, and the prevention of the Company's trade, which has come forth from a two-headed government, and of which there have been all too many examples in previous times, as evidenced by the Contracts made as reconciliation documents thereof, and now (God willing) through a shameful murder of two of the Company's servants together with one severely wounded by Raja d'Houlou's son, Raja Moeda as deputy of his father, and his ahang [uncertain: possibly a title or official position] has been further confirmed, in order once and for all to obtain peace and tranquility both regarding the government and the inhabitants, together with good trade for the Honored Company. 2nd Article This government having been changed in such manner has come upon the person of Raja d'lheer

Thirdly, on each bhaar bessa or Extraordinary Benzoin, large as before, at the rate of four rixdollars. text_translated_detailed: Pabatou [uncertain: possibly a place name] under the protection of an adul karam [a local ruler or official] has placed itself, who is a subject of the Achinese crown, for which reason we shall first have to give Her Honour's Excellency notice in order to obtain orders regarding what must be done in this matter. Therefore I have resolved to undertake the journey from here to Padang tomorrow. For this reason I have deemed it good to have you sail over the sea to Padang, in order to call at the islands of Maros and Inako, and to inquire after the nachoda [captain/master of a ship], who was last there from Padang, of which we have heard that some persons from Padang near Ticou have accosted him and have committed many insolences against him, which evil conduct we shall in no way tolerate in our subjects. You shall therefore carefully inquire of the said Nachoda how matters stand in this regard, so that we may have knowledge of how it came about, proceeded, and ended, in order to punish the evil-doers as an example to others. text_translated_detailed: From Sumatra's West Coast under date 24th May, Anno 1694. Mine and Assay Report of the month of October 1693, to the Honourable Mr. Abraham Bouden, Commander and supreme officer of this Sumatra West Coast, and the council. Honourable Sir, While the works of this gold mine according to my report of the past month of September have made their progress, I shall hereby further report to your Honour in fulfillment of my duty what has been done in this regard, and say that at the beginning of the month the prince stoll [a mining pit or shaft] was worked with 11 pieces of mountain borers, and therewith on the strasses [mining passages] and before the ore-pit gates to be driven in, but the great sickness of the slaves has caused that the number of borers had to be reduced to eight, with which from the 12th to the 24th of the month the work was maintained, and further until the end of this month again with 10 pieces of mountain borers to work, so that in general therein were bored 595 holes, which when blasted with 500 pounds of gunpowder, yielded pure ore amounting to 1900 pounds, which in fine gold [modern equivalent: troy weight] 73:10:— ƒ 1840:12:8, gold 4:12:— ƒ 1686:5:—. Honourable Sir, While the works of this gold mine according to my report of the past month of September have made their progress, I shall hereby further report to your Honour in fulfillment of my duty what has been done in this regard, and say that at the beginning of the month the prince stoll a mining pit or shaft was worked with 11 pieces of mountain borers, and therewith on the strasses mining passages and before the ore-pit gates to be driven in, but the great sickness of the slaves has caused that the number of borers had to be reduced to eight, with which from the 12th to the 24th of the month the work was maintained, and further until the end of this month again with 10 pieces of mountain borers to work, so that in general therein were bored 595 holes, which when blasted with 500 pounds of gunpowder, yielded pure ore amounting to 1900 pounds, which in fine gold troy weight 73:10:— ƒ 1840:12:8, gold 4:12:— ƒ 1686:5:—. Together 78:6:— ƒ 3526:17:8. Also from the 21st to the 25th of this month from the forest were brought 120 pieces. Pure ore obtained: 2050 pounds [lb.], with content as follows, namely. From Sumatra's West Coast [Sumatra's W. Coast] dated May 2nd, year 1738: with fine silver ƒ 2578:2:8, silver 87:2:—, gold 5:2:—, [total] 1819:7:8. ƒ 3997:10:—. In sum 92:4:ƒ

Regarding the deep shafts, I have advanced one more level further in this month. The slaves at the outside work have collected the mine requirements from Sillida and carried the ore obtained here according to the weight, and furthermore while measuring the masonry around the mine's lower post they have steadily continued their work. The plank cutters have cut 30 pieces of wooden poles, with 58 pieces of new planks, of which the carpenters used a portion in making the ramps and repairing the wheels on the wheelbarrows. The charcoal burners have cut 163 pieces of wooden poles for shot plugs and subsequently also burned 395 baskets of wood charcoal, which the smith used in repairing the mining equipment. The basket makers have covered the guard corps with 75 bundles of new rattan and further used 35 bundles of rotting rattan in the manner as follows, namely 23 bundles for baskets, 7 bundles for the hoops of ore barrels, 5 bundles for binding the rattan. From Sumatra's West Coast dated May 2nd, 17[—], 142 pieces. The plug makers have made 110 pieces of new shot plugs from wooden poles. In the hospital there still remain about 10 pieces of both male and female slaves who continue to be seriously ill, except that daily about 15 to 20 pieces who have been afflicted with high fevers and other ailments have had to be excused from work, and of which on the 10th of this month a Kafir woman also died, with which [I remain] your honor's obedient servant, signed W[illem] Roeling (noted at the side) Tambang, dated last March, year 1694: Assay

text_translated_detailed: received per the fluyt the Dove on the 16th of December 1694. From Sumatra's West Coast, the 4th of December in the year 1694. Batavia. To his Excellency the well-born and noble Lord, Mr. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed and Honorable Lords, Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Well-born, strict, earnest, highly esteemed, wise, aforesaid, and generous Lord and Lords. The High Commanding Lords. On the 12th of the past month of October there appeared here from Batavia the fluyt ship the Dove with the yacht the Pepper, likewise bringing Your Excellency's honored letter of the 21st and 28th of September of this year, and on the 28th of October there came the yacht the Gold Fish with Your Excellency's honored letter of the 5th of the same month. Upon these three letters we shall write to Your Excellency with the required due respect and obedience, the necessary report, beginning to say: Since Your Excellency's letter of the 21st of September brought here by the fluyt ship the Dove contains no matter upon which we have to answer Your Excellency, other than that the junior merchant Laurens Phoonsen with his family has hereby landed here, in order, according to Your Excellency's order, to be placed as second at Poelo Chinco in place of the junior merchant Anthonij van Heijst (who has deceased), we have sent him there accordingly. From Sumatra's West Coast, the 4th of December in the year 1699 [note: this appears to be a dating error in the original, likely should be 1694]. We have [confirmed] that the cargo with which the said small vessel was loaded has, according to the bill of lading and invoice, corresponded well in the delivery, and has also been properly received here. Likewise that the two under-masters, one carpenter, three sailors, together with 15 soldiers have come over, for which we thank Your Excellency with due respect and obedience, and with the permission of Your Excellency we shall then proceed to the letter of the 28th of September with the yacht the Pepper sent from Batavia by Your Excellency to us, which we have received.

Your Excellencies, Honored Gentlemen,

Since the junior merchant Van Heijst and Sergeant Cornelis van Bergen have both passed away, they are now unable to make this known. Your Excellencies, Honored Gentlemen, the posts of Aijerhadja, Troussang, and Priaman were abandoned before the arrival of the ships, such that those accounts in the books have been destroyed, and no further expenses are being incurred. To fulfill Your Excellencies' Honored Gentlemen's order concerning the lands of Indrapoura and Majutta, their present constitution of governance, and in what time and manner and way the supreme authority of Indrapoura was transferred from the previous Sultan Mahametchia to the present Sultan Mangsorsa, and how it came about, and in what place and how the aforementioned Sultan now conducts himself, and in what mutual understanding with the other, and also with the Raja of Majutta they are, and how they conduct themselves toward one another, we say that Sultan Mangsorsa holds the governance of Indrapoura, and Raja Adil, together with Raja Ametchia, as vakils [representatives/deputies] of the Sultan of Indrapoura, hold the governance of the Majutta realm, together with the provincial territories, with Raja Adil having the land region of the town of Majutta southward to Banthal, and Raja Ametchia from the town of Banthal southward to Sablas Cartauwen to govern, furthermore that in times of necessity they must help one another with counsel and deed, the realm of Indrapoura being from Sumatra's West Coast on the 4th of December in the year 1694 governed solely by Sultan Mangsorsa, together with his ministers, without the old Sultan Muhametchia involving himself in any governance, but rather as an orang tua (that is) like a respected old man, dwelling in Majutta in the town of that same name and living, and the old and new Sultan, as far as we know, are in good understanding with one another, the time, manner, and way in which the supreme power of

S:r Joannes hoffman tot nogh aldaar sijn verblijff heeft, vermits de boecken onder behoorlijke balance accorderende met het transport doende is, om op te maken, om tot Padang in rade geresumeert te werden, over sulx hij van VEd: ho: agtb: goetheijt versoekt 'tselve hem niet qualijk geliven aff te nemen, dat hier op tot nogh toe geen antwoord heeft gedaan. De twee obligatien ten voordeele der Erffgenaamen van wijlen den lieuten=t Joan Lobs groot 700. gl=s buijten den verloopen intrest door den opperkoopm:, en opperhooft van 't soldij Compt: tot Batavia alhier gesonden, daar over hebben wij den adsistent Simon Calmbergh laten aanspreken, dewelke verclaart die al betaalt te hebben, en derhalven niet geneegen is die ander maal te voldoen, soo heeft den Curateur adlites tot Padang aan ons versoek gedaan, om bij maniere van regten tot de betalinge te komen, 'twelk hem is toegestaan, en staat uEd:e ho: agtb: per het Jaght de peperthuijn daar van nader kennisse gegeven te werden, als mede den E. Baalde opperhooft van 't soldije Conipt: tot Batavia door wien d' obligatien zijn vergesonden. The merchant Hofman, the junior merchant Noblet, and the widow of the junior merchant Van Heijst are to come to Your Excellencies, Honored Gentlemen, Batavia within a few days by the small yacht the Pepperthuijn. The transfer and proper accounting of the merchant Hofman shall be sent to Your Excellencies, Honored Gentlemen, by the Pepperthuijn with all the documents. Concerning the coconut oil, both in receipt and disbursement and accounting thereof, regarding this the yacht the Pepperthuijn Your Excellencies, Honored Gentlemen, is to be informed, since the merchant and subordinate chief at Porto Chinco from Sumatra's West Coast on the 4th of December in the year 1694, Sir Johannes Hofman, still has his residence there, inasmuch as the books are in proper balance according with the transfer being made, in order to be completed, to be summarized in council at Padang, over which he requests of Your Excellencies, Honored Gentlemen's goodness that the same not be taken amiss by him, that up to now no answer has been given to this. The two bonds for the benefit of the heirs of the late Lieutenant Joan Lobs amounting to 700 guilders [modern equivalent: approximately €3,500-4,000 in current value] besides the accrued interest sent here by the chief merchant and chief of the salary account at Batavia, regarding this we have had the assistant Simon Calmbergh questioned, who declared that he has already paid it, and therefore is not inclined to pay it a second time, so the curator adlites at Padang has made a request to us to come to payment by means of legal proceedings, which has been granted to him, and Your Excellencies, Honored Gentlemen, is to be given further notice thereof by the yacht the Pepperthuijn, as well as the Honored Baalde, chief of the salary account at Batavia, through whom the bonds were sent. text_translated_detailed: good profit, but since we were not provided with any desired merchant goods, the same was purchased by foreign traders, who according to their account would bring it to Padang to the Honored Company's market. Raja d'Houlou [uncertain: specific title or name], and his followers remained still somewhat above Sinkel [uncertain: specific location] inland in their dwelling, where he was inclined to end his life. The Company's settlements were mostly all afflicted with sickness, and one had there a master who was not of the greatest knowledge, and also a lack of medicines, which (now from Batavia we have received relief) stood to be improved. There was a murder committed by the Corporal Hans Gerritsz. van Thiel, who sat there in detention, whom we shall have fetched with a Company's small boat, in order to make his trial at Padang, and to receive his wages after work. An English ship had come there to the roadstead and departed again. We have recommended to them the timely preparation both of the business as well as the soldiers' accounts, and in the books, also the sending over of the deceased estates, whose accounts run to Padang, which they promised to follow promptly. On the other hand, such soldiers' accounts were sent to them as ran there on debt accounts, and also a memorandum according to which the business books of the previous year should be corrected in order to accord with the main books. There was a shortage there of rice and coconut oil, and what after the departure of the small fluyt ship the Duifje shall also be brought to them, all detailed in the letters of the 9th of May and 4th of September of the current year from there to the main office, and those of the 7th of June and 25th of August sent thereafter, Your Excellency's High Lordship can review. From Sumatra's West Coast, the 4th of December, Year 1694. —

at Rarago an attack was made, where a large vessel loaded with rice was captured, and they loaded it into their vessels, with which they sailed to Sousou, where their rendezvous is, but because one of these vessels was not well sailed, it was taken by a Company's boat. They also made known that a certain Nachoda [captain] named Intie Timor, who had come from Padang there for trade, after all favor had been shown to him, both in the negotiation of rice, beans, chickens, and so forth, without payment being made for it, this Nachoda, having observed his opportunity, seized five young men in order to carry them away by force. When they wished to resist this violence, two of them were killed, and the other three were brought on board and carried away. The thieves, rovers, and murderers requested that if they could be captured, they would be punished as an example to others, but these have not yet come before us to receive their deserved punishment.

Company, he protested with loud words that he had never been an enemy of the E. Company, nor would he become one, but that over the threatening trouble which truly stood to come upon him, since he did not foresee any remedy in that, he had called his friends to his aid. Upon which General Hoffman assured him that it was merely an imagination, and no difficulties would befall him; he should remain calm. Upon this assurance he left him, but alas, a few days thereafter he was treacherously attacked by night by those of Sompoe, Siettoe Touboualang, and others, killing and wounding some of his people, and Rajah Mamoelia himself barely escaped with his life by flight to the village of Toeboe, which was set on fire by his enemies and destroyed to the ground. This has caused us to resolve, according to resolution of the 8th of October, to send the junior merchants Jordaan Tedingh and Salomon Vermeeren, together with Panglima Rajah, in commission to Priaman, to investigate this and other matters, and if it were possible to settle them, otherwise to refer them to the land council at Padang, as the aforementioned resolution shows. text_translated_detailed: this and other matters, to investigate, and if it were possible to settle them, otherwise to refer them to the land council at Padang, as the aforementioned resolution shows. The affairs of the expelled Rajah Mamoelia at Priaman did not proceed to Sumatra's West Coast on the 4th of December in the year 1694 as one would have wished, so it was referred to the land council at Padang, where the parties appeared, and the matter having been examined, after well five days therewith was brought to a conclusion. Finally, it was arranged in such a manner that Rajah Mamoelia would be restored to the land and the village of Toeboe as chief or rajah during his lifetime, retaining the governance, and after his death, it would then be seen who would be most suitable for the governance, as it was thought that a rajah maningin, insofar as he is as legitimate as the said Rajah Mamoelia, would be designated, setting forth the report made and the business conducted in the land council, herewith enclosed, so that if it please Your Excellency's High Regard, you may be able to read it there in detail. — Soulaccan, from where we have understood that the priest Touanko Atchie, alias Schiaff Borhanadin, is held by the inhabitants as a holy man. In the disturbance when Toeboe was burned and treacherously attacked, he brought the people to a standstill so they would not flee. The Commander therefore had a gift sent to him from his own purse, consisting of a fine bleached muslin and a gift of bethilles [uncertain: type of cloth or ornament], to oblige the said priest to the Company's interest. Bottatenga and Pauw, if they are not likewise engaged in the work of Toeboe, we can say nothing other than that they continue with agriculture. We then proceed to what lies south of Padang, and speak of Majusta and Indra Poura, that since the posts have been established there, little or nothing that can be verified as true has come to our knowledge, as likewise from Aijerhadje and the Sapoeloboua bandaers. Since the Company's settlement at Aijerhadja has been broken up, people want to tell us that the English-minded ones have been in negotiation with those of Seranti Cambang and Sakitang, or whether it is now to take in the English. Of this we cannot assure Your Excellency's High Regard. From Sumatra's West Coast on the 4th of December in the year 1694. — The Commander maintains a rajah Babbaert at his own expense to give him knowledge of what is done in the Sapoeloboua bandaars. This man has had him informed of what the matter is, and also knows to say that those rajahs and pounglous have been in negotiation with some from Indrapoura, but what it would be, he cannot give certainty, and according to common report it would have been the English-minded ones who spoke with them. And we have also recommended to the Panglima of Sillida, together with his pounglous, to keep a watchful eye in that regard. But the said Panglima and his ampat soekous [four clans/families] can give us little knowledge of those peoples, since when they come there, they have no respect for them, and if they want to speak of anything, they are affronted and must depart. Thus we proceed to P[ulo] Chinko, where the trade since the departure of the yacht

text_translated_detailed: Four English ships have been here as well as at Porto Chinco since our writing of the 21st of May of last year, sent to Your Esteemed Honors per the small yacht the Gold Fish, namely the Northampton twice, both going to Bancaul and returning to Madras, the Dorothy, which came directly from England and departed for Bengal, the ship the Caeton toward Bancaul, etc., having provided themselves with water, firewood, and refreshments, their journey to Bancaul, Madras, and Bengal proceeded. We shall shortly be able to report to Your Esteemed Honors the findings of the cargo brought with the small yacht the Pepper House and the ship the One Horn (which arrived here with Your Esteemed Honors' writing of the 27th of October on the 18th of September) only after they are completely unloaded, since they are not yet entirely unloaded. The Lassam salt, with respect to its large white grain, according to what the inland merchants say, is worth 5 rixdollars [modern equivalent: approximately €15-20 in current value] more than the fine white salt, and since it is also not dry but moist, the inlander here prefers the coarse black salt, because it is completely dry: this is, Esteemed, highly honored gentlemen, as much as we can write about the salt, we hope that Your Esteemed Honors will have issued orders concerning this. The trade would be in a desired state here if the cargo could have been arranged and fulfilled in prices and quantity according to our request made, namely red salempouris [uncertain: type of cloth] bleached, blue brown moris fine bleached, red Parkallen, 986 guilders 10 [modern equivalent: approximately €6,000-7,500 in current value]. From Sumatra's West Coast, the 4th of December in the year 1694. would be; then we would have been able to provide the following goods, namely 38 pieces of cannequins (as before) at 16.

From Sumatra's West Coast, dated the 4th of December in the year 1694. We are of the opinion that one should satisfy Raja Mamoelia, in order to draw back to us the mountain peoples who remain after this abominable deed, and thus with their gold and edible goods bring them to us, as we understand that they are not inclined to pass through the lands of such villainous inhabitants, and consequently the Esteemed Company would thereby be deprived of the gold and edible goods. — To satisfy Raja Mamoelia, we think this shall consist of making the perpetrators of the villainous deed pay all that Raja Mamoelia and his people have lost hereby, together with restoring him and his people to his land and village as it was before this lamentable deed, and then if there is anyone who might have any claims against Raja Mamoelia, let those be brought before the land council, to hear the parties and administer justice as is proper, whereby the parties must be satisfied. We believe that with the foregoing (insofar as it has come to our knowledge) we have paved the way for you to remove this abominable deed, being able thereby to do that which you shall deem necessary to the advantage of the Esteemed Company and to the settlement of the deed, in reason consisting: but if you encounter any matters in which our opinion is needed, you must make that known to us by writing, as when we shall support you with our advice. — Tintoe Nantingi being the upper part of Oulaccan where Raja Amat, the son of Raja Mamoelia, has his residence and rule, we have from Sumatra's West Coast, dated the 4th of December in the year 1694, understood that through this committed abominable crime it is entirely abandoned, and the peoples have fled, wandering here and there, you shall therefore be able to have to ensure that those peoples come back to their places of residence. And since you shall be at Priaman, you must through all reasonable means endeavor to remove the war that is in the mountains, between the village of Sompoe there, with those of Batipoe, Bongitanjon, and Bittella, as the Esteemed Company is accused of lending a hand in this, because those of Sompa (a village from which the Malay merchant Soutan Amaas is born) have engaged with hand grenades against their party (a weapon not customary among them, by which 5 men would have been killed), they of Sompa cry out that they have received them from the Esteemed Company, and that with the Company's might they shall be strengthened against their enemies: a matter as little known to the Commander as

text_translated_detailed: — Priaman, Esteemed Commander and Council. After we obtained our departure from Your Esteemed Authority on the 12th of this month, we set out from the West Coast of Sumatra under date of the 4th of December, Year 1694, according to the contents of the instruction also given to us, at three o'clock in the afternoon on horseback on our journey to Priaman, in order to conduct there such matters as Your Esteemed Authority had been pleased to command us through the aforementioned instruction, and we arrived at the falling of evening over the river of Cotta Tenga, where we remained that night in a fisherman's hut, and the following morning at the breaking of dawn we set out on our journey again, so that on that very same day we arrived safely at Priaman. We understood from the assistant Hoffman (who was there for the purchase of rice) that Panglima Raja had appeared there the day before, and that everything there was again in peace and quiet, just as the aforementioned Panglima Raja appeared on the 14th of the same month in our pagger [fortified compound] and confirmed the foregoing, as well as that someone on his behalf had been sent to the warring parties to urge them further toward peace and quiet, believing that everything would turn out well, for which reason we resolved to send out the next day the Corporal of the Bugis with 2 soldiers and the Pounglou Cauwal [local chief] in order to summon Raja Mamoulia of Tobo, Maradjalila of Oulaccan with their Pounglous, as well as those of Sjinto and Lobos Illong to us, so that we might settle and resolve the matters in question as soon as possible, and just as the aforementioned Corporal departed on the 15th of the same month and would on the 16th of the same month, with the approval of Panglima Raja, send a Raja Dunarra, brother-in-law of Sultan Becopia, with a token that had been sent from us to the aforementioned Sultan, to make known to him that we had appeared here,

The reason why Intje Kerim returned to Simon Bouwa was to purchase rice and paddy there for the maintenance of the force being assembled, and once loaded with these, to follow to Sousou. After their departure of 8 days, Intje Kerim sailed toward Sousou and Rarago. Besides this violent enemy, the Raja had, for the third time, yet another general, Sonobasta, chief Pounglou in the upper lands of Naij, dwelling in the village of Bombotjolij, who, without any legitimate cause, had pursued him most severely with weapons for five months already, whereby about 200 of his subjects had been killed. The cause of this war, as the Raja informed us, is this: a certain subject of Sionobasta had carried away two slaves and given them into the keeping of a subject of Raja Silebo on Rarago under the condition that they would be kept safe, so that they would not come to light. The carrier having departed, after the lapse of a month he returned and demanded the slaves back. However, the keeper, having already sold them, answered that the slaves had died. The carrier, subsequently finding the contrary, as one slave was seen with another person to whom he had been sold, from Sumatra's West Coast under date 4th December in the year 1694, went back to the keeper and demanded payment for him. But the keeper, still persisting in his previous statement that they had died, the carrier, entirely enraged, departed again, and after 6 days returned with some other persons and murdered the keeper and his people in his house. Raja Silebo had no knowledge whatsoever of this deed before—

But the keeper, still persisting in his previous statement that they had died, the carrier, entirely enraged, departed again, and after 6 days returned with some other persons and murdered the keeper and his people in his house. Raja Silebo had no knowledge whatsoever of this deed before it was committed, and when he was informed by his people that Sionobassa's men had fallen upon the village and murdered some subjects, he became entirely distressed, fearing that Sionobassa had thereby declared war on him. For this reason, he also took up arms and sent his people out to go on the offensive. However, this enemy, being too powerful in numbers, had so weakened his force that he could no longer maintain his position against them, and on the other hand, if Moare Padang should come again, he would be entirely defeated with all his people. For this reason, he urgently begged us that, now being in the utmost need, we would secure him. We, having heard his complaints, answered that what concerned Intje Timor, Moare Padang, and Simo Toalang would be faithfully made known to the Esteemed and respected Commander and Council, and when that happened, we did not doubt that the one human robber, as shall be obtained, would receive his deserved punishment, and the violent ones Moare Padang and Simo Toalang, thwarted in their evil intentions, would be prevented from their robbing and plundering. The Raja must also seek good means to make peace with Sionobassa, so that upon the return of the aforementioned Moare Padang, from Sumatra's West Coast under date 4th December in the year 1694, he would be in a position to keep him away from the land. To this, he replied to us that he had already presented peace to Sionobassa several times, but the latter had never been willing to incline toward it, urgently requesting us again that we would protect him, for Sionobassa would not dare undertake anything against the Esteemed Company, nor would he refuse its orders, seeing that he was a fellow ally of the Esteemed Company. We, having thus understood that Sionobassa was also in contract with the Esteemed Company, promised him that we would call at Naij in passing to Maros, summon Sionobassa before us, and seek to restore peace. The Raja should meanwhile undertake no further offense whatsoever against the said Sionobassa, so as not to cause further disturbance among those peoples on account of our negligence. Furthermore, we recommended to him to send, as soon as possible, a good quantity of rice, paddy, and oil to Baros. In this and otherwise, the Esteemed Company would come to order him. He promised to risk everything, notwithstanding that the sea was made unsafe by the said robber birds Moare Padang, intending to dispatch the next morning four vessels with paddy and old coconut shells (in place of oil, which they did not have) and other provisions which they had in abundance under the escort of his old brother Farcha, and furthermore always to supply this office abundantly, and also wished to—

And concerning the chief pounglou Sionobassa, they say that when our arrival at Rarago was understood, out of fear that the Company had come to wage war with Raja Silebo, to pursue him, he had withdrawn deeper into the mountains.
