text_translated_detailed: the true [account from] Sumatra's West Coast, under date of the 4th of December in the year 1694. [He] had not known the cause of this deed, or had not learned in time enough that the murderers were already in the hands of Sionobassa, to receive their punishment, had sent out his [men] for vengeance, who then also killed some subjects of Sionobassa. Sionobassa, seeing that Raja Silobo had taken up arms against him, had also prepared himself against that, and thus they had come to blows with one another, and many had fallen on both sides. Among others, the son of Sionobassa had also been killed, which had made him greatly embittered against Raja Silobo, and thereupon the war had also begun more fiercely. This matter being thus impartially examined by us, for this people lived in friendship with both disputing parties, and gladly saw (as much as we could perceive from them) that the dispute be settled, and they could be united again, we gave them complete credence. But in order not to burden this matter on the one side, nor on the other, we attributed these disturbances, or confusion of misunderstandings on the part [of both], and recommended to them that someone from their pounglous should go to Sionobassa, and tell him that he should cease from the war against the allies, and appear in person with us, needing in no way to fear that any harm would befall him or his from our side, for he was just as much an ally of the Company as Raja Sileboo was, and also had not sinned against the Company in this matter. This terrible bloodshed had sprung solely from their mutual misunderstandings, and in order to prevent that the Company's allies would not be so miserably murdered without any guilt, we had come here, to place ourselves in the name and on behalf of the Company as mediators between the parties, and to settle this dispute

text_translated_detailed: Gunung Limau [Gunung Limau:] lay one mile's distance from this anchorage, and on land they had thrown up a solid palisade furnished with much large and small firearms positioned at the river's mouth with wooden and bamboo obstacles making it impassable. The paths everywhere were set with foot traps and covered deep pits with belly traps, fortified trenches made impassable. They forced all the surrounding villages such that all their goods, whether slaves or other merchandise, were delivered to no one but their master. Recently, fifteen slaves and just the day before our arrival a vessel with rice had been sent to them, which was actually the reason they feared, and they lacked no vessels. We, understanding this in good faith, held this in reserve until our return, rowed back aboard, but first had instructed our intermediaries to pay good attention to the Malay's behavior so that upon our return we could give a good report of it. We encouraged them instead to use their own weapons, in which they were experienced, against their enemies with manly courage, and by doing so they would ward off the violence. To this end, and out of no enmity—which surprised us that there was concern about this, since we well knew that the Honored Company had never done such a thing to its allied partners and had remained so long faithful, would not do so—we had come here and also gave them a staff with silver fittings to serve as a token of friendship, with which they then departed on their way. On the 13th of the same month in the afternoon, the chief Pounglou Siwatjoe came back together with our interpreters and reported that Sionobassa had been very pleased at their arrival, had shown great friendship toward them, and after they had delivered their message, had accepted it and promised that within 3 days he would come to us together with the other Pounglous and his 2 sons. Upon this, the chief Pounglou Siwatjoe made known to us that a great number of Atchinders and other foreign traders had fortified themselves at Gunung Limoe [Mount Limoe], allied with those of Simon Bouwa, and had threatened him that they would attack at first light and destroy his villages, salt refineries, and other things, because he was an ally of the Honored Company. We, basing ourselves on this disclosure as if we knew nothing of any Atchinders or Malays, asked him when they had arrived there and what their purpose was. text_translated_detailed: had threatened him that they would attack at first light and destroy his villages, salt refineries, and other things, because he was an ally of the Honored Company. We, basing ourselves on this disclosure as if we knew nothing of any Atchinders or Malays, asked him when they had arrived there and what their purpose was. He said that some had already been living at Gunung Limoe for some time, and shortly thereafter several more Malays had come, and now they were strong with 9 vessels, at Simon Bouwa and Gunung, trading in slaves, paddy rice, and other goods. This they had also sought at Naij, but since they were confederated with the Honored Company and according to the contract obligated with the Honored Company from Sumatra's West Coast under date of the 4th of December in the year 1694, to trade exclusively and to the exclusion of all other foreign traders, they had rejected this and thereby made themselves enemies. We, having been thoroughly informed beforehand by the common people regarding this matter, as is noted under date of the 24th of April, could perceive their fickleness from this, but in order not to give them suspicion, we did not wish to make any mention of it and kept the same reserved until the time would come to present their apparent confederation before their eyes. We answered him therefore that the enemies must be held back by force outside their land boundaries, and if they came along the shore, we would also not let them go free. With this he seemed satisfied and departed again. On the 14th of the same month in the morning we saw from the ship toward the side of Gunung Limoe a strong party of armed Malays show themselves on the shore, but after some feigned grumbling without advancing further toward us they departed again. From this it became clear to us that they were more intent on us than on the inhabitants of Naij, as was said. We therefore kept ourselves always in good defense. On the 17th of the same month, the appointed day from yesterday having expired,

Early in the morning, three islanders came to us in a canoe and informed us that five jaloors [type of vessel], well-manned and equipped with firearms, had landed at Goenong Situlij, and there did great damage to their coconut palm trees, requesting that we would come to their aid and offer resistance to the robbers. Whereupon we resolved, since it was in the wind, to row there with the tinang [type of vessel] well-manned. We would forbid them, as they were friends, from damaging the coconut palm trees on pain of arrest. But regarding the notorious robbers, we would endeavor, if possible, to get them into our power and bring them in. We thus rowed with the tinang along the shore, and when they caught sight of us, they ran off with full sails toward us. We dropped our anchor to wait for them and to gain the weather gauge of them. However, they passed us by, and having recognized us, they fired 5 cannons at us, and sailed off to windward (without any offense or defense being made by us). We pursued them with the tinang (notwithstanding our best efforts with sails and rowing), but we could by far not catch them, for these jaloors are nonetheless small and light, carrying two masts, and by means of the help of the oars they shoot forth with a very swift speed. text_translated_detailed: (was signed) Fredrik Weijniger. Mines and Assay report of the month of June in the year 1694, to the Esteemed and Honorable [Heer] of Sumatra's West Coast under date the 4th of December in the year 1694. Esteemed and Honorable Mister Abraham Bouden, Commander and supreme officer of this Coast, and the council. Esteemed and Honorable Mister On the Prince Stoll [mine shaft] the work in this month has been continuously advanced with 12 pieces of miners, and by the breaking of 198 holes, in which was consumed 450 pounds of gunpowder, and thereby obtained in pure separated ore, a quantity of 1900 pounds, containing in silver and gold with the last grain 73: 10:—, valued at ƒ2820:6:4, with the last grain silver 10: 10: 9 ƒ 1766:8:2, gold 2:15:9, 1053:18:2, together 73: 10:— ƒ 2820: 6: 4, as before. Meanwhile the old shaft has been provided again with 4 pieces of new passages or adits, and 6 thereof heavy props [supports], in order to place the workers in no danger when climbing up and down. Furthermore the people at this work from the 28th until the last day of this month have gone into the forest, and have extracted 364 pieces of the felled mine props [wooden supports], in order to use the same, as needed, at the works. In the deep stoll [mine shaft] one has advanced a layer further for the ore. The slaves at the outside work have continued their ordinary labor regarding the carrying of the mine's needs, subsequently from the mine pagger [embankment] to the Sillidase River the undergrowth and forest along the way, which is kept unsafe by the tiger, has been cut down. In the meantime also, because they otherwise had no work, stones have been carried to the masonry of the mine below the pagger. The charcoal burners have delivered 210 pieces of large baskets of wood charcoal, which the smiths require for the making and repairing of the tools and forging. From Sumatra's West Coast under date the 4th of December in the year

text_translated_detailed: Advice from our letter, of which we have not been able to send the copy sooner. From Bengal, the 18th of January, Anno 1694. Batavia. To the Most Noble and Esteemed Mister Wilhelm van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of Our India. The Honorable Commanding, Respected Mister P. de Fluyt Bovencarspel and Gentlemen received on the 29th of March 1694. Our most recent respectful advices in duplicate were sent by the ships Belois and Boswijk, dated the 26th of November of the past year, and we do not doubt that Your Esteemed and Respected persons will have received them safely with the preservation of those vessels, so that we shall excuse ourselves from sending their copy at present; and now we shall again let this serve as an accompaniment to the fluyt Bovencarspel, the reason for which the bearer of this brings, along with the delay of the 3,035 sacks of saltpeter which we recently advised had come from Patna and were underway, and had been arrested in the warehouse for so long, until we obtained the release from necessity only with a gift to the regents present there; and subsequently only on the 30th of December of the past year appeared in port, which has remained in our hands contrary to expectation until now; the cargo of the same we shall specify at the foot of this, and now let flow in below, and bring to Your Esteemed and Respected knowledge, with what and which vessel on the sea in December of the past year to Ceylon and the fluyt the Crab on the 15th current to the Fatherland have been dispatched, it appears subsequently from Bengal on the 18th of January, Anno 1694, what good vessels Usaman, goods in the past month of December of the past year the yacht and the Lady Susanna, and vessel on the Sea, toward Ceylon, likewise on the 15th of the same month over said Island the fluyt the Crab toward the Fatherland have been dispatched, as first on the 8th of December of the past year the yacht the Lady Susanna for Persia 2,436 pieces sick classes.

As for the remainder, I said, when we hopefully still encounter the return ships, we shall endeavor to dispatch them as quickly as possible to Ceylon [Colombo], which time alone shall have to teach. Having previously mentioned how the Great Mogul had caused the trade of Christians to be prohibited throughout all his lands by issued mandate, so shall we, to briefly set forth for your High Excellency the reasons which moved the aforementioned monarch thereto, present the aforesaid order, which was granted to the duan over Bengal, hereinafter inserted, reading as follows:

Translation: Copy of the Hasbul Hoccum [Hasb-ul-Hukum: decree] from the Chancellor of the Realm, Assetchan, on the 21st of the month Siam ma delouwel [uncertain: month name] of Bengal, under date of the 18th of January in the year 1694, in the 36th year of the King's reign, or the 20th of February 1693, granted to the Lord Duan Kiffaitchan in Dhecca [Dacca], received on the 6th of April following thereafter. After the compliments, Kiffaitchan, be in good health, and know by these presents that His Majesty has seen from the writing of Attimaetchan, duan over the souba [province], Gouserath, that in the past and present year, ships belonging to Malla Abdul Gaffoer and several other merchants, together with all loaded goods and merchant wares, have been taken by Christians, whereupon the captains of the Dutch, English, and French were summoned by the wackanawies [uncertain: official title], or day register keeper, and were told that together they must devise a means to seek out those pirates, and since they were unknown to them, each one was to prepare a ship, all of which the aforementioned captains refused to undertake, whereupon the duan (to compel them) prohibited trade to those nations in Surat [Surat], which being also made known in Hindustan, they would then certainly submit to it.

From Bengal under date of the 18th of January in the year 1690, 4 war ships under the esteemed Commander van den Bergh as mentioned appeared here, only in the short term again toward Ceylon and Coromandel, with the Ceylon and Coromandel goods for those places being prepared to return, Oost Zouburgh and the Scheldt, and the others here for the first time also remain to watch, to observe the designs of the French, the more so as it could easily happen that more ships of that nation coming directly from France, and learning of the surrender of Pondicherry, came here to seek their hiding place. text_translated_detailed: Per the fluyt [flute ship] Bovencaspel received on March 29th from Bengal under date January 10th, Year 1694. Batavia To the Most Highly Esteemed Lord, Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies, Your Excellency's great honor, most esteemed, highly commanding lord and gentlemen. Our arrival with the main body of the war fleet at the roadstead of Bellasoor, we have respectfully brought to Your Excellency's great honor's knowledge by our most recent humble [letter] of the 14th of the month just passed, as likewise by an appendix dated the 15th and [another date] appended to the same submissive letter, the capture of two enemy vessels named L'Escuille and Legaillard within the Ganges by our two detached ships of war under the Vice Commander Willem Burggraaf. And since that missive has not yet departed, but rests at Oughly and apparently will be dispatched together with this one, this letter shall serve only to notify Your Excellency's great honor most humbly that I have since then, with the boat of the ship Domburgh from Bellasoor, proceeded to Bengal under date January 18th, Year 1694, to visit the situation of the positioning exactly. Finding that the French, should the Indian powers wish to undertake it, might come out in order to advance their journey from here more easily than could be observed from elsewhere, since they would then have to pass under the shot of our ships. And since the honored Director Arnoldus Muijkens, by missive of the 22nd of the month just passed, of which the copy Your Excellency's great honor shall receive by the next [opportunity], makes known that the fluytes [flute ships] Dieren and Ysselt urgently needed to be employed again in the merchant service, and therefore required that we, in place of the Ysselt, together with Zalland, add yet another of our ships of war, the Vice Commander, I thereupon immediately caused the ship Hontholredijk to depart from the Bellasoor roadstead for that purpose,

By the fluyt Bovencarspel there have been sent to Your Excellency's most esteemed three of our humble and subordinate letters sent from Bengal under date of the 15th of February in the year 1694, dated the 14th of December, enlarged with an appendix under date of the 15th, as well as the 3rd and 27th of January last, from which, together with the documents attached thereto, we hope will have become clear to Your Excellency's great esteemed upon receipt hereof, both the capture of two enemy keels, L'Escuille and Le Gaillard, accompanied by yet another smaller one called the Postilion, as well as that we have deemed it good to have the ships Domburgh, Honsholredijk, Zallandt, and Castricum remain here for that purpose, just as the one and the other shall again be evident from the accompanying Copies, in the absence of the originals (from which we nevertheless sincerely hope the contrary:) which we have also deemed it advisable to have accompanied by such attachments as may in that regard contribute somewhat to greater elucidation.

text_translated_detailed: Following this, we find ourselves through the departure of the ships Oostsouburgh and the Scheldt, on the 3rd of the current month from the Bellasoorse roadstead toward Coromandel and so forth, entirely without means. Since you, upon our departure from Batavia with this fleet on the 21st of September 1692, were likewise provided with the Instruction by the Esteemed Excellency the high Indies government dated the 20th of that same month, decreed upon me and the council, you cannot be unaware how their High Excellencies have been pleased to order therein, in case the enemy should remain within the Ganges, to station there such a number of warships as against theirs was deemed redoubtable and sufficient, in order to be able to attack them coming out with advantage, and so forth; furthermore, to employ the remaining vessels of this fleet in such manner as the greatest service of the general Company should come to require; I shall then merely say briefly in this: that we, in fulfillment of the first, in order to keep the enemy ships now within, L'Escuille and De Gaillard, accompanied by yet another small one called the Postillion, in a state of rest, by the successive resolutions of last December of the year just past, as well as the 11th and 17th of the current month, have unanimously determined to hold a number of four ships, for which purpose the following have subsequently been selected: Domburgh, Honsholredijk, Zallandt, and Castricum, as well as in conformity with the other, and also with their High Excellencies' further order, dictating: that in the month of February of this year, from here above the saltpeter, which is now not being supplied, some goods for Coromandel,

From Bengal under date of the 15th of February in the year 1698 [note: likely a scribal error for 1694], and whereby you will also be more capable, upon meeting some enemy vessels, of achieving the objective of our esteemed commanding lords. text_translated_detailed: After some enemy vessels had sunk in these waters, the governor of that place, where Your Excellency found yourself at such a time, judged Your Excellency's presence here to be unavoidably required again. You shall not allow yourselves to be lacking in your duties, but after having received the proper orders beforehand, you shall return to Herwijs [Hugli] as quickly as possible, so that, as circumstances require, you shall be properly combined in time against the enemy's departure. This foregoing matter thus briefly set down for Your Excellency's information, there remains nothing else but to earnestly recommend to Your Excellency collectively to guard yourselves well against all encounters with the enemy that may occur, always also regarding as an important point that in the provisions, ammunition, equipment, and goods the required management be observed and that the pertinent accounts of consumption be properly kept. While I hereby conclude, I commend Your Excellency to God's holy guidance and with the wish for a prosperous and safe journey, I remain Your Excellency's well-disposed friend, signed: S. V. d. Bergh [Simon van den Bergh]. In the margin: on the ship Domburgh [Domburgh], lying in the settlement within the Ganges near Kasserije [Cassimbazar], the 28th of January 1694.

Register of all such letters and papers as today by the Esteemed Mister Director Arnoldus Huijkens and Councillor at Hugli are dispatched to the Most Noble Lord Governor-General Willem van Outhoorn and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies at Batavia, namely per the fluyt ships Walenburgh and Hobree, No. 1. An original missive to the aforementioned Your Honour of today's date. 2. Three extracts, namely two from the missives dated the 26th of January and the 15th of last month by the chief merchant Theodorus de Haese and councillor in Patna, and one by the chief merchant Pieter van Dijxhoek and councillor from Cassimbazar to Hugli. 3. text_translated_detailed: Per the fluyt ships Walenburgh and Hobree, received on the 21st of June 1694, per Walenburgh from Bengal, the 26th of March, Anno 1694. No. 16. Original open missive by as before to the Esteemed Lords Guardians of the Poor at the city of Batavia under today's date. 17. Ditto by as before to the chief merchant the Esteemed Gerrard de Heere and Councillor in Japan of this date. 18. Invoice and bills of lading of the cargo loaded in this vessel. 19. Cost account thereof. 20. Three licence letters, whereby it appears what the chief merchants of these vessels are permitted to carry outside the hold from here to Batavia. 21. An extract of a secret missive by the Esteemed Mister Director Arnoldus Huijkens, of the 6th of this month to the Company's war fleet to the Esteemed Commander Simon van den Bergh at Hugli in Bengal on the 16th of March, Anno 1694 (was signed) A. Cranendonk, so stated. Batavia. To the Most Noble Lord Governor-General Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General and Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Noble and High Commanding, Honourable Lord and Lords. On the 15th of last month we have Your Honour's Excellency most respectfully advised of our writing per the ships Dieren and Borssenburgh, ditto regarding the arrival of the fluyt ships Hobree and Walenburgh, no saltpetre from Patna in place received, a foolish and ridiculous pretext of the King's duan there. From Bengal, the 26th of March, Anno 1694. Per the ships Dieren and Borssenburgh aforementioned, and at the foot of the same also made known the safe arrival here of the ships Hobree and Walenburgh, of which the copy is sent herewith (because it has been sent in duplicate), in Your Honour's Excellency's good pleasure shall excuse, and now subsequently set down what since the aforementioned last outgoing advices has again occurred regarding the matter of trade in this directorate, first beginning with the difficult Comptoir [trading post]

On the 15th of last month, we made a beginning with the contracting for the homeland, and resolved to provide the merchants, as mentioned, from our cash box, and the proceeds from Bengal on the 26th of March in the year 1694. We intend to send the last ships this season, and wish to increase somewhat more. However, despite all the diligence applied to this, no more has been found than four chests. Therefore, the remainder that your esteemed gentlemen now receive with these shipments of that product will in total make 83 chests, all of very good quality, and a certain quantity of opium of good quality, which we have negotiated here in place, and for which we also humbly request your esteemed gentlemen to be pleased to write to us, not only how the now-passing batch of the mentioned sleeping sap has been found, but also the previous one sent by us in the course of this season, in order that we may be able to rest assured regarding those which are used for the inspection of it, and likewise, in order that when there is any deficiency regarding the quality, we may distinctly know whether that sap was negotiated at Hooghly or Patna. — Since our cash box is not sufficiently provided for the undertaking of the new contracting for the homeland at present, we have made known to your esteemed gentlemen with respect in our last letter of the 15th of last month. However, since the best time for this, notwithstanding the shortage, continues to pass daily, and the governor in place, as mentioned before, has given assurance on behalf of the Honored Company regarding the procurement of cloth that he will render all possible assistance, we have resolved to proceed with that great work nonetheless, and to enable the merchants to make a beginning, to provide as much money for it as the little that is available at the cash box here, strengthened by what continues to proceed daily from the merchant's accounts, from the merchant's accounts to allow, in hope of a good remittance of cash, as can be seen from the accompanying resolution. Regarding the demand of 800 rolls of sailcloth, we have satisfied the supply of those cloths. The bearer of this will deliver to your esteemed gentlemen from Bengal on the 26th of March in the year 1694. We hope that at the end of this month or beginning of April the expected remittance of cash from the homeland via Ceylon will arrive, so that we can then further satisfy the money that the merchants still have to their credit regarding their assumed quotas. As the accompanying letter dated the 16th current, a copy of the resolution taken thereon on the 16th current in council here, your esteemed gentlemen being pleased, will show in detail. And on which day we have also charged the merchants with your esteemed gentlemen's further provisional demand of 60 packs of raw sailcloth, and 60 dozens of fine, middling, and coarse photasses for India, where the 80 packs of garasses included thereunder, no one has yet been willing to accept. Therefore, we shall make further effort toward this, and shall spare no means to send the same to your esteemed gentlemen also in the next season.

text_translated_detailed: 20th of February: Recently received matters have been respectfully deferred to Your Excellency's great judgment, and we shall await Your Excellency's further high and esteemed command for our guidance in deep respect. The yacht Lieutenant Martensdijk has not been heard of anywhere here up to now, which causes us some concern regarding the equipment and goods that Your Excellency's great judgment had shipped in that small vessel, especially concerning the iron and wheel ropes that are stored there for this fleet, the Bengali ordinary [rope] being quite weak for that service, as they are commonly employed for it. Therefore we most respectfully request Your Excellency's great judgment to supply us by the next [opportunity] with a dozen of each of the aforementioned rope works, by means of which we would then, should it happen (which God forbid) that the aforementioned yacht fell entirely behind, still be adequately equipped to save ourselves in the present difficulty. Meanwhile we shall refrain from petitioning for any equipment goods from Hooghly [Hugli] for so long until we obtain some further certainty regarding the aforementioned small vessel from Bengal, dated 26th March, Year 1694. In order also, as far as is possible and within our power, to keep our hand on the ships and their doubling [maintenance/repair], we likewise request most humbly that, together with the aforementioned ropes, by order of Your Excellency's great judgment, there may be assigned to us for each ship 30, or together 120 pieces of medium-sized bay planks of 1½ inches [modern equivalent: approximately 3.8 centimeters], since we are completely out of stock of that sort and entirely depleted. In the month of October of the year just past, a certain English ship appeared within this river, which claims to belong to a new Company recently restored in England, but is regarded by its countrymen here in Bengal as an interloper, and no communication whatsoever is held with it; the same having run aground so dangerously upon entering this river that one could see nothing but a complete shipwreck approaching, it was, out of regard for our mutual alliance, by the Vice Commander Burggraaf and our other captains, then lying in garrison near Kasimbazar, helped again from the dry ground with all possible assistance and entirely out of that danger, but instead of showing a due acknowledgment for the received favor, he has not hesitated to harbor two deserted sailors from the ship Oostsouburgh [East Souburgh], of which one, as is reported, has again gone missing and has already departed in January of the year before last with one of the English vessels Charles the Second or the Samson from Bengal, dated 26th March, Year 1694. However, through the esteemed Director Sluijkens, restitution of the other has been requested, and they did indeed give full assurance of this at first, but since then upon further insistence they have flatly refused in such a particular manner that it sufficiently made clear that they would not lack the means to seduce more of our ships, where possible, which is truly not only with regard to the friendship shown but also in view of the fact that they always wish to be regarded as our friends and allies, and with which appearance they particularly know how to disguise themselves well in time of need.

text_translated_detailed: On the 20th of September in the year 1694, the overseers of Bombay [Bombalia/Bombahia], while returning here, encountered near the highlands of Pondicherry [Pondij] a certain English Company ship called the Atchinese Merchant [aatchinsen Coopman], which they could not refrain from assisting in their utmost need and danger of being lost, with a small anchor and half a length of cable rope. For this, the amount of rixdollars [ro/a] 42:1 3/8 was received by the Company here in the Company's cash box of that nation, amounting to rixdollars 424:13 3/30. Accompanying this is the memorandum from that matter signed by our vessel's skipper and bookkeeper, together with a translation of what the English agent, knowing of such matters, has therefore communicated to us for Your Esteemed Honors' consideration and reflection. — Having thus far answered Your Esteemed Honors' esteemed letter on the simplest points in all humility, we shall proceed further to that which principally concerns the entire account here: setting aside the fulfillment of our promises regarding the affairs of the Esteemed Jan Pit, made in the most recent humble letter of the 26th of March of this year sent from here to Your Esteemed Honors. We have therefore, in accordance with this, on the 8th of April sent the documents and papers to the Esteemed Dijxhouk, and thereupon ordered that he answer them according to Your Esteemed Honors' intention, upon which we have received such documents in return as the copies attached hereto can humbly demonstrate, and to which we ourselves, insofar as they do not concern us, defer to your favorable judgment; and in order to further add our part thereto and to demonstrate more clearly what the state of that matter is, Your Esteemed Honors shall in all humility be presented in repetition with four extracts from as many of our successive letters, the first of the 13th of September in the year 1690, sent per the Yacht Wijk op Zee to Your Esteemed Honors

Whereby it has then become clear to us, among other things, that the friends there for the issuance of the documents for free trade (mentioned herein) have been compelled to contribute still to the King's customs authority 3,500 rupees, and to his son 350 rupees; and since the customs authority has thereby also desisted from the claimed salt tax [uncertain: original text], just as he would otherwise well have been compelled to levy, we hope that Your Excellency's Lordship will be able to bear this much better for the service of the Esteemed Company, than if we without this, to that harmful levy, which in time has become a law, and unequally more would have been imposed, than to an irremovable yoke would have remained bound. text_translated_detailed: From Bengal, the 20th of September in the year 1694. Batavia. To the High and Esteemed Lord, Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General and E.E. Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Esteemed High commanding, respected Lord, and Lords. Received the Jaeltje de Zusanna on the 23rd of September 1694. From Your Excellency's esteemed high honored missive dated the 28th of June last, separately addressed to me, I have read with obligation, and it pleased me that Your Excellency had been willing to take, regarding various matters which Your Excellency had made known to me by my separate humble letters in the past season, and likewise I thank Your Excellency humbly regarding the complete orders, how I might regulate myself on behalf of the Company, concerning the prevention of our friends from transporting saltpeter, and further, or rather principally, regarding the purchase and transport of that salt in Patna. As to the first matter, we shall continue only to divert each one from it as much as is possible by means of persuasion, as well foreseeing without bad consequence to make ourselves subject to it, yet we cannot well prevent it otherwise; and as to our own affairs in Patna, regarding which Your Excellency's esteemed shall now come to understand by our public writing what kind of improvement for the better has recently come to us regarding the previous vexations, in such a way that I refer to that in this matter, from here hoping that such shall continue for many years. Upon Your Excellency's esteemed favorable consent to grant transport to those persons who from France and service show themselves inclined to come to us, three of them now go by the Jagtje de Zusanna thither, who have freely presented their service, namely Pieter Wijn Corporal, Marijn Roe sailor, and Jeroen Rosschel soldier. Upon Your Excellency's esteemed favorable consent to grant transport to those persons who from France and service show themselves inclined to come to us, three of them now go by the Jagtje de Zusanna thither, who have freely presented their service, namely Pieter Wijn Corporal, Marijn Roe sailor, and Jeroen Rosschel soldier. From Bengal, the 20th of September in the year 1698. However, we have not assigned them any wages, but promised Your Excellency's esteemed that you would do so according to their merit, when request may be deducted therefrom, 8 rixdollars [modern equivalent: approximately 8 guilders], which we have counted out to each of them from the Company's cash, to provide some clothing for their bodies, of which they were poorly provided, it being apparent that subsequently still more will present their service, and when according to Your Excellency's well-given order, we shall nevertheless take care that no greater number be placed on each vessel than we shall deem serviceable for the security of the ships, upon which Your Excellency's esteemed will be pleased to be gracious. In our aforementioned public letter, Your Excellency's esteemed shall find spoken what ships we presently have here for the lodge, and how the Jagtje de Zusanna is fitted out, to depart now only thither at present, and this because we have no greater supply of saltpeter on hand, but since we now expect a strong shipment to arrive shortly, we hope to be capable, by the beginning of the month of October, to remit to Your Excellency's esteemed by the Bombahia or the Ijsselt (there we can only serve ourselves so early with, because the vessels lying below, cannot be ready for the lodge before mid-October, and consequently only in December can be made ready to be sent:) another strong shipment, and

text_translated_detailed: Since we are expecting a strong shipment to arrive shortly, we hope to be in a position, by the beginning of the month of November [expanded: gber = November], to remit another strong shipment to Your Excellency's esteemed lordship per the Bombahia [ship name], or the Ijsselt [ship name] (where we alone can serve you so early, because the flat-bottomed vessels lying low cannot be ready for the warehouse before mid-November, and consequently can only be prepared in December to be sent): and at the same time as much merchandise as possible on the Batavian and Japanese account, as shall be feasible, having the sailcloth and the amphioen [uncertain: possibly a type of fabric or commodity] now cannot be brought to a greater quantity than is contained in the accompanying invoice, because we have received nothing yet from Patna of the first, and of the sailcloth consequently a brave quantity [considerable quantity] has already been supplied to the warships, whereby our stock has been strongly diminished; we keep the weavers at work to supply that shortage, and if it is feasible, Your Excellency's esteemed lordship could order another batch of 150 to 200 rolls from us next time. For the granted communication of that which Your Excellency's esteemed lordship has deigned to write to the Honored Commander Simon van den Bergh, I find myself obliged to thank Your Excellency's esteemed lordship most humbly; the business which on that account we have conducted with the aforementioned honored Commander here, and what had to be decided upon the advice of the pilots regarding the positioning of the fleet from Bengal on the 20th of September in the year 1694, while the ships lying under Ilha dos Galos [island name], in case of need could not take another secure retreat behind the north corner of the same island according to that which Your Excellency's esteemed lordship had proposed in that regard, since among other things the grounds there had been taken up too much, and that place had thereby become unsuitable; mention is made of that in our aforementioned humble public letter now departing,

text_translated_detailed: From Bengal on the 29th of October in the year 1694, arrived at the river, which would truly be a regrettable matter, yet as Your Excellencies with your high wisdom will best know, what weighs most heavily here and what must be done or left undone, so Your Excellency's esteemed order to the aforementioned Mr. Commander van den Bergh can provide the best clarification regarding this. text_translated_detailed: Your Excellency's Honors: regarding those matters which could be discerned concerning the pice [a small coin], we have respectfully provided clarification to Your Excellency's Honors according to our promise in a letter of the 20th of January last, which Her Excellency's Honors have been able to give regarding the pice rupias and the procurement of flax in these lands; and since Your Excellency's Honors are undoubtedly familiar with the nature of the aforementioned currency in its entirety, we shall refrain from making any further mention thereof in the favorable reception, but regarding the flax, we shall briefly say that in Patna [Pattera] there appears to be no prospect of being able to collect anything from it, as they themselves cannot determine whether it grows well there, as Your Excellency's Honors may observe from the accompanying Extract of their letter dated the 17th of October, but to Cassimabasaar [Kasimbazar] the friends are of the opinion that, in case there were a good European land cultivator there who understood the cultivation of it, one could well obtain a good quantity thereof, which Your Excellency's Honors is likewise humbly requested to observe from the more detailed accompanying extracts of the Cassimabasaar letters of the 7th and 23rd of October, appended hereto for that purpose. Besides the 80 chests of opium (as mentioned at the beginning of this letter) shipped in the fluyt [a type of ship] Borssenburgh, that vessel has also been given the parcel of confiscated goods aforementioned, examined by those who understood such matters and properly packed in 9 chests in the presence of the commissioners, comprising the entire cargo of that vessel, as well as the quantity of saltpeter and pots of butter per the yacht Castricum, proceeding as follows: In the fluyt Borssenburgh for Batavia. 232,000 lb. saltpeter - in 1,600 sacks. 8,199: 6:5. 3,048: 8: 7. 6 packs. 360 pieces.

Per the ship Borssenburgh, which now proceeds in the same manner as we did with the Bombay, although to us there has come back again three French military men, who since then have come over to us, by name Jean Lamars de Leuran French drummer, Le Cuije of Brest, soldier, and Allexis Le cof of Cuslij, having each received for their needs also 8 rixdollars [modern equivalent: approximately 8 Dutch guilders] on account. text_translated_detailed: 5th of June, and yet from there per the yacht the Susanna the last on the 28th of the same month, all of this year, and moreover yet on the 23rd of August there per the ships Schoondijke and Borssenburgh in answer from Batavia have received an extract of that which Your Excellency's honorable esteemed in date the 8th of July 1693, this direction concerning, thereupon to the high Indian government have deigned to write, upon all which this humble then respectfully in reply as well as to dutifully demonstrate the state of this direction, and how it has proceeded regarding Your Excellency's honorable esteemed commerce in the same since our first humble submission per the return ship the Crab under date the 15th of January last year has taken place, being directed, we shall in all humility beforehand our regret say, that we with a particular regret, from the esteemed writing of the Honorable and Lord Extraordinary Councillor of India, and Governor Thomas van Rhel, and councillor to Ceylon [Cheijlon] dated the 11th of May of this year, and per the Ijsselt aforesaid brought here, has come to light, how the aforesaid return ship the Crab, as well as the shipment from Surat and Persia have had the misfortune of arriving at the aforesaid place too late, in order to be able to repatriate at the more convenient time with the keels ready there, in such a way that His Excellency has been compelled to divide that vessel with its full cargo of the finest goods onto some other ships, in order to equalize the risk somewhat, to have dispatched toward Batavia; and as we therefore have reason to believe that His Excellency, Your Excellency's honorable esteemed from there, our humble letter, per the aforesaid return fluyt doubly departed, will have shared, so we consider it in the favorable well-being of no necessity to let the copy of that this time.

P: S: aan voorschreve missive Terwijle het geensints seker gaat, dat hier een persoon sal gevonden worden, die sigh op het insamelen van vlas verstaat, zoo zoude evenwel bij VE door een inlander daar van wel een preuve konnen genoomen werden, en ook een exactelijk werden onderstaan, wat quantit:t dat 'er van 't selve naar ruijge Calculatie wel soude Rrija te procureren wesen, in Cas die suijveringh goet wierde bevonden om zulx mede nogh naar 't vaderlandt over te konnen schrijven Extract missive door den opperkoopman d'E Pieter van Dijkhoek, mitsg:s den Raad tot Cassimabasaar in dato 23:en October a:o 1694. aan d: E:r direct=r Arnoldus muijkens, en den Houglijsen raad naar herw=ts gecarteert. En ons omtrent het vlas informeren wat 'er van zal konnen vallen, soo het goet is, sal de quantiteijt algroot zijn, om dat men dat hier bij na soo veel souw konnen doen zaijen als men ook begeert, altijt in de landen die daar toe bequaam zijn, des daar van voor dat het besoght is, om de gedughte swarigheeden van dat het tekort en te dun zou zijn, ook geen Calculatie altoos te maken is.
text_translated_detailed: it seems to give hope that flax could well be prepared and obtained there, in case there was a farmer who understood the preparation of it, so we shall upon Your Excellency's suggestion on the incoming ships make inquiries about it, and having found the same person, Your Excellency shall receive him, in the hope that this undertaking will then be of good success, meanwhile we shall communicate this advice to the High Esteemed gentlemen majors in the most humble manner. P.S. to the aforementioned letter: While it is by no means certain that a person will be found here who understands the collection of flax, nevertheless by Your Excellency through a native a sample of it could well be taken, and also an exact inquiry be undertaken as to what quantity of the same according to rough calculation could be procured, in case the purification were found to be good so that this could also be written to the fatherland. Extract of letter by the chief merchant Mr. Pieter van Dijkhoek, together with the Council at Cassimabasaar [Kasimbazar] dated the 23rd of October in the year 1694, to the Esteemed Director Arnoldus Muijkens, and the High Council forwarded hereafter. And let us inquire of you regarding the flax what will be able to come of it, so if it is good, the quantity will be large, because one can sow as much of it here as one also desires, always in the lands that are suitable for it, therefore before it is sought, because of the feared difficulties that it would be scarce and too thin, also no calculation can always be made.

Extract of a letter from the merchant chief Theodorus de Haase together with the Council from Patna [Pattena:] dated the 17th of August in the year 1694, written to the Esteemed Director Arnoldus Muijkens together with the Council toward the homeland. We cannot determine whether good flax can be obtained here, much less in what quantity, therefore we find ourselves for the present unable to provide Your Esteemed Excellency with a fuller explanation of this matter, but we shall not fail to conduct further investigation into it, and shall inform Your Esteemed Excellency of the findings in due time. Register of the Papers which on this day by order of the Esteemed Commander Simon van den Bergh and the Council of this war fleet are dispatched per the ship Castricum [ship name:] to the Most Esteemed and Honored Lord Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Namely: No. 1. Original letter from the aforementioned Commander and Council to the aforementioned Most Esteemed Excellencies dated this day. 2. Copy secret thereof by the aforementioned Commander dated the current date per the Yacht de Bombahia [ship name:] to their Excellencies' great respect sent by letter. 3. The register of papers together with the aforementioned letter dispatched. 4. Extract from the letter by the aforementioned Commander van den Bergh of the 28th of August 1694 to the Esteemed Arnoldus Muijkens at Hooghly [Houglij:] concerning the shipment of one hundred fifty pots of butter in the ship Castricum. 5. Bill of lading of the cargo loaded in the aforementioned vessel for Batavia. 6. Two copies of resolutions taken in the broad council of this fleet received per the ship Castricum on the 20th of January 1695. From Bengal dated the 24th of November 1694, that is the 3rd and 16th current, containing the establishment and fortification together with the discharge of certain ship's officers. No. 7. Muster roll of the ship Castricum. In the war ship Domburgh, lying in garrison within the Bevrier [Bevier:] the Ganges, near the barracks on the 16th of September 1694. (was signed) Thomas Paas, secretary.

Batavia. To the Most Esteemed and Honored Lord Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Esteemed, most greatly respected, stern and commanding Lord and Esteemed Gentlemen. Following the departure of the most recent humble secret letter from the Commander dated the current date per the Yacht de Bombahia, of which the copy is enclosed herewith, we were between the 2nd and 3rd thereof at night brought by the Vice Commander Burggraaf Your Esteemed Excellency's greatly respected original letter of the 23rd of August of last year, together with all such attachments as pertained thereto and were noted in the register, for the communication of which we take the honor to thank Your Esteemed Excellency most heartily, and to which the Commander finds himself especially obligated in the most humble manner, for that Your Esteemed Excellency has been pleased to grant him so graciously his discharge from this office and license to travel to the homeland, to which end sending to his Excellency his replacement the aforementioned Vice Commander Burggraaf to continue to exercise authority over this garrison, which then in conformity therewith is to be transported tomorrow, and the aforementioned his Excellency is then to be presented publicly to the people, whereby the Commander will have the opportunity to remain at Hooghly for a few days to From Bengal dated the 24th of November in the year 1694, refresh himself and from the ailments which his Excellency, through the prolonged time spent aboard, has contracted, to recover somewhat, until such time as the ship Zealand is made ready and its cargo is loaded, so that then as soon as possible with that vessel the journey to Batavia may be undertaken. In the meantime the Castricum, within a few days, is to be dispatched ahead loaded with such goods as the bill of lading shall dictate, of which the quantity of butter pots, on the proposal of the Director Muijkens, have also been shipped therein, for all such reasons as the enclosed extract from the letter written by the Commander on the 28th of October to Hooghly can humbly demonstrate, to which we respectfully defer to avoid needless repetition. Your Esteemed Excellency's most gracious orders concerning various matters to be observed by us in the aforementioned letter are set forth, which we shall follow from our obligation with strict exactitude, just as indeed all our ships have already been brought under the barracks, hoping with God's help in time and while to be capable of achieving Your Esteemed Excellency's intention, so that the designs of the enemy everywhere remain fruitless and may be thwarted, to which end and in order to provide the Vice Commander Burggraaf with the necessary elucidation of all that pertains thereto and especially this garrison, the Commander shall, in accordance with Your Esteemed Excellency's command, place into his hands all such papers as can be of any service thereto.

text_translated_detailed: Since this train of supplies cannot be recovered before the closing of our account books, we shall provisionally charge the aforementioned quantity of gunpowder to the Bengal directorate by invoice, from where it can then be credited back in due course at Ceylon or Malabar. For the sent recruitment of 13 European and 30 native soldiers, we likewise cannot fail to thank Your Excellency's great and esteemed lordship most heartily, and it shall be arranged alongside the reduction of the crew from the ships Castricum and Zalland, which now depart from this supply train, in such a manner that the 4 vessels remaining in service can each be allocated their competent number of 150 men, and of which Your Excellency's great and esteemed lordship shall receive the pertinent muster rolls with the arrival of the Commander, while in this matter only those of the ship Castricum have been sent ahead. The 2 pieces of metal cannon of 18 pound [approximately 8.2 kg] ball, which erroneously ended up in the ship Domburgh at the Coromandel Coast and remained there due to the shortness of time, and which by their unsuitability are not needed here in the fleet, we have already had transferred to the ship Zalland, so that this vessel may carry them further overseas. Herewith we shall conclude this in deep respect, and commend Your Excellency's great and esteemed lordship with the Company's weighty concerns to the safe keeping of God's providence, while we remain with deepest dutiful respect (signed) Your Excellency's great and esteemed lordship, most obedient and obligated servants (was signed) S. V. d. Bergh, W. Burggraaf, Leendert Broek, N. oole Lambert Cleijn, P. d' Heer, and N. Blom. In the margin it stood: In the warship Domburgh anchored within the Ganges near Casserije [Kasim Bazar] on the 16th of September in the year 1694.

text_translated_detailed: From Bengal dated the 24th of November in the year 1694. Register of papers sent on this day by the Esteemed Vice Commander Willem Burggraaf, supreme commander over the Company's war fleet in Bengal, and consigned to the High and Esteemed Lord Mr. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General and the Esteemed Lords Councillors regarding the state of affairs in India to Batavia. Register No. 1: Original letter from the Lord Vice Commander Burggraaf and Councillor of the war fleet to their Esteemed Excellencies at Batavia dated the 29th of November in the year as stated. 2. Copy of resolution drawn by the Vice Commander and council of the war fleet dated the 21st of November as aforesaid. 3. Copy of register of papers by the Esteemed Lord Simon van den Bergh, General Receiver of the Company's domains at Batavia and former Commander of this war fleet, delivered to the Vice Commander Burggraaf upon the transfer of command, in order that he might regulate himself accordingly. 4. Request from Adriaan van Heijst in the war ship Oostsouburgh [East Castle] lying in garrison before Casserij [Kasim Bazar], dated the 29th of September 1694, was signed Adriaan van Heijst, Secretary of Batavia. To the High and Esteemed Lord Mr. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Well-Esteemed, greatly respected, severe, most generous and high commanding Lord and Lords, With the safe arrival of the Vice Commander Burggraaf in the river of Bengal, which occurred on the 4th of this month, and the delivery of your Well-Esteemed highly honored orders dated the 23rd of August of the previous year to the Lord Commander van den Bergh, the Vice Commander from Bengal, dated the 24th of November in the year 1694, accordingly, following the same on the 17th day thereafter, presented by the General Lord Commander to the people in this fleet, in order to assume command over the same and the vessels lying in garrison in place of his Excellency, and in which the Vice Commander also hereby declares that he will apply all possible diligence to bring about your Well-Esteemed complete contentment and satisfaction, upon which your Well-Esteemed may fully rely. And we in all respect shall continue to say that the Lord Commander van den Bergh, upon the transfer of command, has also delivered to the Vice Commander such papers as the copy register attached hereto under No. 3 shall be able to show to your Esteemed Excellency, to which we are devoted in all subordination, just as we also are to the resolution in copy under No. 2 attached hereto, and drawn by us in council here upon the recommendation made by the aforementioned Lord Commander and with communication from the Lord Director at Hooghly [Hugli] dated the 21st of this month, regarding the appointment of a secretary, since it was the pleasure of the Lord Commander van den Bergh to permit the former secretary of this fleet, Thomas Maas, his discharge to accompany him to Batavia, humbly requesting that our action in this matter may be accepted by your Well-Esteemed as well done, and our appointed secretary Adriaan van Heijst, with your Well-Esteemed Excellency's favorable disposition, regarding his request now also being forwarded under No. 4, be confirmed; as not doubting that the same shall bring your Well-Esteemed Excellency complete contentment in that office and sufficient service to the Company, and the Lord Commander van den Bergh, upon safe arrival, your Well-Esteemed's pleasure permitting, shall be able to provide further information regarding him.

text_translated_detailed: of the Lord Commander van den Bergh's great respect, in order to prevent all misfortunes and to keep the people as much as possible from running away and from becoming unhealthy (which otherwise would be to be feared from one side and the other), may be pleased to favor their petition in this regard, and pardon us that we, from the aforementioned considerations, with communication from the Lord Director and council at Hooghly, upon further order and the pleasure of your Well-Esteemed Excellency's great respect, have taken the liberty to resolve to put this provisionally into effect, under hope and trust that your Well-Esteemed Excellency's great respect, with much wiser and more experienced judgment, will better understand the misfortunes that might otherwise arise from this than our limited understanding, and will not take it amiss of us, in which case we also from our hearts wish to be strengthened by your Well-Esteemed's pleasure to be able to send a large portion of the salted meat and bacon to this or that place, and in doing so to be able to unload some of our vessels which are overstuffed with it, each remaining provisioned for only 7 months, just as the ships Oostsouburgh and Schondijke from Batavia are provisioned, which we under the correction of your Well-Esteemed Excellency's great respect trust will be sufficient to undertake the greatest voyages in India, should the occasion arise. This is, Well-Esteemed Excellency, Lords, all that has occurred since the transfer of command to the Vice Commander Burggraaf in the fleet lying in garrison here, and which we dare not fail to bring to your Well-Esteemed's knowledge, but from our subordinate duty have thought it necessary to do so, with humble petition that whatever in this may come to conflict with our hope and thoughts against the high honored pleasure of your Well-Esteemed Excellency's great respect, your Well-Esteemed may be pleased to overlook through the fingers

text_original: Van Bengale Den 29=en October A=o 1694. revier quamen te arriveren, dat waarlijk een spijtelijke saek zoude zijn, edogh gelijk VEd:e agtb:s met hunne hooge wijsh:t best zullen weten, wat hier ontrent het swaarste wegen, en gedaan, off gelaaten worden moet, zoo zal VEd:e agtb: g'eerde ordre den h=r Command:r van den Bergh voorsz:, daar omtrent de beste verlightinge konnen geven. Met brenger deses 't Jaght de Bombahia varen nu wederom naar derw=ts 4. stux fransche gedeserteerde persoonen, namentlijk sve Le fran van Belliele germeijn Brigon, van Vrantes Bastiaen Bejoe van Brest, en Charles Cherie, van gernezee, mitsgaders dan nogh een timmerman van't Jaght de seijmour, zijnde den Enterloper tot ons overgekoomen, genaamt Christiaan Sleijk van Bijllevelt, op Conditie als die nu Iongst p:r 't Jaghtje de Zusanna zijn versonden, hebbende mede ijder op hand ro/a 8. genooten, om tot VEd:e agtb: naright te dienen; en desen hier mede dus kortelijk affbrekende, zal ik naar gantsch nedrige groete, en diep respect verblijven (onderstont) Ed=e Hoogh gebiedende, achtb=re heere, en heeren, uw Ed=e aghtb=e onderdanigen en gehoorsamen dienaar (was getekent) H=s Muijkens (in margine) Houglij in Bengale adij 29:en october A=o 1694. — Register der papiren, die op heeden door d' E. Heer Simon van den Bergh, Command=r van sE. Comp:s navale krijgsmaght, p=r 't Jagtje de Bombahia werden afgesonden, aan den hoogh Edelen Heere, m:r Willem van outhoorn, guvern:r gener:l, en d' Ed: heeren Raden van Nederlands India, namentlijk N=o 1. originele secrete missive door bovengen=de h:r Command:r op heeden aan welgem:te haar ho: Ed:s gecarteert.
text_translated_detailed: From Bengal, the 29th of October in the year 1694. [We] arrived at the river, which would truly be a regrettable matter; however, as Your Excellencies with your high wisdom will best know what weighs most heavily here and what must be done or left undone, Your Excellencies will be able to give the honored Commander van den Bergh the best clarification regarding this matter. By the bearer of this, the yacht the Bombahia sails again toward there with 4 French deserted persons, namely Sieur Le Fran from Bellisle, Germain Brigon, from Nantes Bastiaen Bejoe from Brest, and Charles Cherie from Guernsey, as well as a carpenter from the yacht the Seymour, being the Interloper [privateer vessel] who came over to us, named Christiaan Sleijk from Bijllevelt, on the condition as those were recently sent per the small yacht the Susanna, each having also received on hand 8 rixdollars [modern equivalent: approximately 8 guilders], to serve Your Excellencies; and thus concluding this matter briefly here, I shall remain with most humble greeting and deep respect (understood) Your Excellency's commanding, honorable lord and lords, your Excellency's obedient and obedient servant (was signed) H. Muijkens (in margin) Hooghly in Bengal on the 29th of October in the year 1694. — Register of the papers which on this day by the Esteemed Lord Simon van den Bergh, Commander of the Company's naval military force, per the small yacht the Bombahia were sent to the highly esteemed Lord, Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of Dutch India, namely No. 1. original secret missive by the aforementioned Lord Commander on this day to the aforementioned their high Excellencies dispatched.

text_original: Van Dambij onder dato 15=en Maart A=o 1694. om den sulthan Ingalaga, ten welken eijnde den Pang: Pringabaija zijn hoop, en vertrouwen naast godt geheel:jk op zijn Ed:t, en op VEd=e goede gunste steld, op dat den sulthan Ingalaga weder na de vervallen stadt Jambij mag komen, en deselve daar door tot sijn vorige florisantie geraaken. Edogh Jngevalle den sulthan Ingalaga op Jambij niet komt te verschijnen, zoo zal zekerlijk, de aansienlijke mogentheijt van d E Comp:, en ook van haar Ed:e ho: agtb: daar door merkelijk komen te verminderen, mitsg:s mijn persoon geheel op den dool- wegh geraaken Eijndelijk heeft den Pangerangh Pringabaija niet anders aen den Ed:le h:r direct:r generaal Joan van Hoorn te senden, dan alleenlijk een handrottingh met goud beslagh, met eerbiedigh versoek dat dese geringheijt, als een gemeen bloem takkje met aangenaamheijt gelieft te accepteren. — Translaat van een maleijtse missive door Pang: Pringabaija tot Jambij gesz: aan den gewesen koningh van Tambij sulthan Ingalaga ontfangen op Batavia den. . . april A:o 1694 Dese onderdanige gebiedenisse van zijn maijesteijts geringen zoon Pang: Pringabaija werd bij dese missive opgeofferd voor de voeten
text_translated_detailed: From Jambi under date the 15th of March in the year 1694, concerning the Sultan Ingalaga, to which end the Pangeran Pringabaija places his hope and trust wholly next to God upon his Excellency and upon Your Excellencies' good favor, so that the Sultan Ingalaga may come again to the fallen city of Jambi, and thereby bring the same to its former flourishing state. However, in case the Sultan Ingalaga does not come to appear at Jambi, then certainly the considerable power of the Company and also of their Excellencies' high honor will thereby come to diminish notably, and likewise my person shall come entirely onto the wrong path. Finally, the Pangeran Pringabaija has sent nothing else to the Esteemed Lord Director General Joan van Hoorn than merely a hand-woven cloth with gold mounting, with respectful request that this trifle, as a common flower sprig, may be pleased to accept with favor. — Translation of a Malay missive by Pangeran Pringabaija at Jambi sent to the former king of Jambi Sultan Ingalaga received at Batavia in April in the year 1694. This humble submission of his Majesty's lowly son Pangeran Pringabaija is hereby offered at the feet [of the recipient].
